questions.original_query: What are the major flavonoid compounds found in Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers, and what are their associated biological properties?

query.text: What are the major flavonoid compounds found in Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers, and what are their associated biological properties?
query.answer: The major flavonoid-type compounds reported in Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers/calyces are mainly the anthocyanins delphinidin-3-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside, followed by delphinidin-3-glucoside and cyanidin-3-glucoside. In addition, flavonols such as gossypetin, hibiscetin, and their glycosides have been identified, and quercetin and luteolin are also reported among its phenolic/flavonoid constituents. Their associated biological properties include: - Antioxidant activity, especially for the major anthocyanins. - Radical-scavenging and anti-inflammatory activities for flavonols like gossypetin and hibiscetin. - Antioxidant and antimicrobial effects associated with quercetin and luteolin-containing extracts. - Inhibition of LDL oxidation and protection against oxidative stress, suggesting anti-atherosclerotic potential. - Antihypertensive and cardioprotective effects attributed in part to anthocyanins and other flavonoids. - Hepatoprotective and anti-diabetic activities linked to flavonoid-rich fractions. - Anti-cancer and apoptosis-inducing effects reported for anthocyanin-containing fractions. In short: the key flavonoids are anthocyanins and flavonols, and they are mainly associated with antioxidant, antimicrobial, antihypertensive, anti-diabetic, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, and hepatoprotective effects.

The major flavonoids reported in hibiscus flowers are mainly:

- <cite id="b66c495d-0">anthocyanins derived from cyanidin</cite>
- <cite id="20cd223b-0">glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol</cite>

Associated biological properties include:

- **Antioxidant activity**: <cite id="20cd223b-2">H. sabdariffa is rich in anthocyanin compounds that provide antioxidant activity.</cite> Also, in hibiscus petals, <cite id="b66c495d-0">the antioxidant activity increased in proportion to the anthocyanin concentration</cite>.
- **Anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects**: <cite id="2dc24790-0">delphinidin-3-sambubioside has been linked to inflammation, glucose metabolism, angiogenesis, and cell proliferation pathways</cite>.
- **Anticancer potential**: <cite id="20cd223b-3">Anthocyanins from Hibiscus sabdariffa calyx attenuate in vitro and in vivo melanoma cancer metastasis.</cite> The same review also notes <cite id="20cd223b-3">anticancer properties</cite>.
- **Antimicrobial/antiparasitic effects**: <cite id="20cd223b-3">antimicrobial, antiparasitic and anticancer properties</cite> have been reported for hibiscus constituents.
- **Cardiometabolic and protective effects of hibiscus extracts**: hibiscus preparations have shown <cite id="dbc6e56d-0">antihypertensive, antidyslipidemic, hypoglycemic, body fat mass reduction, nephroprotective, antianemic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory</cite> activities, which the review states <cite id="dbc6e56d-0">are associated with the phytochemicals found in HS</cite>.
- **Quercetin-related effects**: in hibiscus, quercetin is one of the common biocompounds, and <cite id="2dc24790-0">QRC analysis demonstrated interconnected targets spanning multiple pathways ... with a particular focus on pathways related to cancer</cite>.

In short: the key hibiscus flower flavonoids are **anthocyanins** (especially cyanidin- and delphinidin-based forms), **quercetin and kaempferol flavonols**, and **catechin/epicatechin**, and they are mainly associated with **antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, antimicrobial, and cardiometabolic protective effects**.

questions.original_query: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery for Poland syndrome?

query.text: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery for Poland syndrome?
query.answer: Safe anaesthetic management in Poland syndrome starts with <cite id="57b63f53-1,ab2df539-3">careful preoperative examination, intraoperative monitoring, appropriate choice of general anaesthetic technique, and planned postoperative pain management</cite>. Preoperatively, clinicians should assess the extent of <cite id="21e8776f-3,a2407141-3">pectoral/chest-wall deformity</cite> and screen for <cite id="21e8776f-1">associated anomalies such as dextrocardia, atrial septal defect, hemivertebrae/scoliosis, renal aplasia, hypospadias, inguinal hernia, and situs inversus</cite>, because <cite id="57b63f53-2,f7f327dc-1">patients may have important ventilation-related problems</cite>. Intraoperatively, <cite id="57b63f53-1,e7d9b9b8-0">general anaesthesia with controlled ventilation can be used safely</cite>, but <cite id="57b63f53-0,57b63f53-3,57b63f53-5">reported susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia means special preparation, avoidance of triggering agents, and careful anaesthetic selection are prudent</cite>. Postoperatively, <cite id="a2407141-4,ab2df539-7">close respiratory observation is essential because prolonged ventilation and difficult weaning may occur when chest-wall mechanics are abnormal</cite>.

without_scope.text: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery?
without_scope.answer:
## Preoperative assessment

Safe anaesthetic management begins with <cite id="c9ba77cd-1,c9ba77cd-2">a structured preanaesthesia evaluation that uses medical records, a patient interview, and a physical examination, and should be completed before the day of surgery in high-risk patients</cite>. At minimum, <cite id="c9ba77cd-3">the focused examination should assess the airway, lungs, and heart, with documentation of vital signs</cite>. Preoperative investigations should not be routine for everyone; instead, <cite id="449db235-2,c9ba77cd-5">tests and consultations should be ordered selectively when they are needed to guide or optimize perioperative management</cite>.

## Patient preparation and risk reduction

A safe plan also requires <cite id="45b25045-1,4e3193b7-0">review of medical and psychological conditions, concomitant medications, and possible substance use disorders</cite>, because these factors affect anaesthetic risk, analgesic needs, and postoperative recovery. Fasting instructions are essential: <cite id="ee2daf6e-3">clear liquids may be taken up to 2 hours before elective anaesthesia</cite>, while <cite id="ee2daf6e-0,ee2daf6e-1">breast milk is typically allowed up to 4 hours before, and nonhuman milk, infant formula, or a light meal up to 6 hours before; fatty meals require about 8 hours</cite>. These steps help reduce aspiration risk and improve perioperative safety.

## Intraoperative management

During anaesthesia, <cite id="39d31cf6-5">qualified anaesthesia personnel should remain present throughout general anaesthesia, regional anaesthesia, and monitored anaesthesia care</cite>. Core monitoring must include <cite id="fa890b38-0">continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature during all anaesthetics</cite>. In practice, this means the anaesthetic technique, airway plan, fluids, haemodynamics, and drug dosing should all be adjusted in real time to the patient’s physiology and surgical course.

## Postoperative care

After surgery, recovery-area care should continue to emphasize safety: <cite id="8ef8fc19-1">oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature should be monitored in the postanaesthesia period</cite>. Analgesia should be <cite id="4e3193b7-0">multimodal, individualized, and guided by validated pain assessment tools, with nonpharmacologic options and patient education included</cite>. Postoperative nausea and vomiting should be addressed by <cite id="af102036-4">identifying high-risk patients, reducing baseline risk, and planning both prophylaxis and rescue treatment</cite>. Finally, <cite id="8f1fd506-0">discharge criteria should be designed to minimize the risk of central nervous system or cardiorespiratory depression after discharge</cite>.

In short, the essential perioperative considerations are <cite id="c9ba77cd-1,c9ba77cd-3,ee2daf6e-3,fa890b38-0,8ef8fc19-1">careful preoperative evaluation, proper fasting and optimization, continuous intraoperative monitoring, and structured postoperative surveillance</cite>, together with <cite id="4e3193b7-0,af102036-4">individualized pain and PONV prevention strategies</cite>.

questions.original_query: What does the evidence from randomized controlled trials indicate about the effects of early versus delayed neuraxial analgesia on labor duration and delivery outcomes in nulliparous women?

query.text: What does the evidence from randomized controlled trials indicate about the effects of early versus delayed neuraxial analgesia on labor duration and delivery outcomes in nulliparous women?
query.answer:
Evidence from randomized controlled trials in nulliparous women indicates that <cite id="1202adda-6">giving neuraxial analgesia early in labor did not increase the rate of cesarean delivery, and it provided better analgesia and resulted in a shorter duration of labor.</cite> In nulliparous women undergoing labor induction, a later randomized trial likewise found that <cite id="1202adda-0">early-labor neuraxial analgesia does not increase the cesarean delivery rate compared with late epidural analgesia in nulliparas undergoing induction of labor.</cite>

Systematic review evidence focused on nulliparous women is consistent with these trials: <cite id="ac09f410-0">there was no increased risk of caesarean delivery or instrumental vaginal delivery for women who received early epidural analgesia at cervical dilation of 3 cm or less in comparison with late epidural analgesia.</cite> A broader review of randomized trials similarly concluded that <cite id="8c5f5b99-0">even when neuraxial analgesia is administered early in the course of labor, it is not associated with an increased rate of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery, nor does it prolong the labor duration.</cite>

So, overall, the RCT evidence suggests that in nulliparous women, early neuraxial analgesia versus delayed neuraxial analgesia <cite id="ac09f410-0,8c5f5b99-0">does not worsen delivery outcomes such as cesarean or instrumental vaginal delivery</cite> and <cite id="1202adda-6,8c5f5b99-0">does not prolong labor; if anything, some trials found a shorter labor duration with earlier analgesia.</cite>

questions.original_query: How do the different structural components of the periodontium work together to support and protect teeth from damage and microbial infection?

query.text: How do the different structural components of the periodontium work together to support and protect teeth from damage and microbial infection?
query.answer: The periodontium is the tooth-supporting apparatus made of <cite id="90f35b1a-0,90f35b1a-8">gingiva, cementum, the periodontal ligament (PDL), and alveolar bone</cite>. <cite id="1f60a27d-0">The junctional epithelium of the gingiva is firmly attached to the tooth and forms an epithelial barrier against plaque bacteria</cite>, while <cite id="d1cda059-1,d1cda059-0">gingival crevicular fluid helps maintain the junctional epithelium and contributes to the antimicrobial defense of the periodontium; it also contains serum-derived components and leukocytes</cite>. On the root surface, <cite id="609f9d55-1,609f9d55-5">cementum provides the attachment of the tooth to the alveolar bone by anchoring periodontal ligament fibers</cite>. Those fibers are crucial because <cite id="609f9d55-0,1f60a27d-1">the PDL connects cementum to alveolar bone through collagen bundles/Sharpey’s fibers and acts as a shock absorber</cite>, helping dissipate chewing and biting forces. Finally, <cite id="22f8e741-5">the alveolar bone helps maintain the teeth within the jaws</cite> and <cite id="22f8e741-1,22f8e741-6,22f8e741-7">remodels in response to occlusal forces, with resorption and new bone formation adapting support when loads change</cite>. Together, <cite id="1f60a27d-0,d1cda059-1">the gingival seal and immune-rich crevicular fluid limit microbial invasion</cite>, while <cite id="609f9d55-1,609f9d55-0,1f60a27d-1,22f8e741-5">cementum, PDL, and alveolar bone form a load-sharing attachment system that stabilizes teeth and protects them from mechanical damage</cite>.

In the center, <cite id="2399fe14-0">the pulp contains connective tissue, blood vessels, and nerves</cite> and <cite id="2399fe14-0">mediates immunologic defense</cite>, helping keep the tooth vital. Around the root, <cite id="53dbd355-1">the radicular dentin is covered with cementum</cite>, and <cite id="53dbd355-2">the cementum of the tooth root provides attachment between the root proper, and the surrounding periodontal ligament (PDL) and alveolar bone of the socket</cite>. These root-supporting tissues are part of the periodontium, which <cite id="53dbd355-0">consist[s] of four components: cementum, the periodontal ligament (PDL), alveolar bone, and gingival tissue</cite>; within it, <cite id="8c735011-0">gingiva ... functions as a protective mechanical barrier</cite> and <cite id="8c735011-3">the periodontal ligament ... provides stability to the teeth and absorbs mechanical stresses</cite>. Together, these parts cushion biting forces, hold teeth in the jaw, and create barriers and immune responses that help prevent damage and infection.

query.text: How do the different cochlea shape categories relate to variations in the trajectory of the cochlear centerline?
query.answer:
The cochlea shape categories are defined by how the <cite id="6f1566a1-0">cochlear centerline</cite> changes vertically along its course.

- <cite id="fe772b89-0">A sloping shape has an upward trajectory without any significant downward trend.</cite>
- <cite id="3b73bc58-0">The intermediate shape follows a slight upward trajectory after the RW, which then follows a slight decrease.</cite>
- <cite id="1f80b774-0">The rollercoaster shape follows a more pronounced up-and-down path: it rises after the round window (RW), transitions to a downward trajectory, and then returns toward level.</cite>

So, the categories correspond to increasing complexity of the centerline trajectory: <cite id="fe772b89-0">monotonic upward (sloping)</cite>, <cite id="3b73bc58-0">mild rise then fall (intermediate)</cite>, and <cite id="1f80b774-0">marked undulating rise–fall pattern (rollercoaster)</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do different shapes relate to variations in the trajectory of the centerline?
fully_underspecified.answer: Different shapes are closely tied to how their centerline moves through space: <cite id="S23">local geometry and centerline trajectory jointly define the global shape</cite>, and <cite id="S21">changing the centerline of one shape to the centerline of another shape without changing the local geometry induces a shape change of the former shape into the latter</cite>. In geometric terms, <cite id="S17">the centerline shape is completely determined by its curvature and torsion, for given boundary conditions</cite>; <cite id="S24">curvature measures the rate at which the curve bends, while torsion measures the rate at which the curve twists out of the plane of curvature</cite>. So, straighter shapes correspond to low curvature, <cite id="S19">constant non-zero curvature and zero torsion</cite> gives a circular trajectory, and <cite id="S19">constant curvature and constant torsion</cite> gives a helical one.

questions.original_query: How do health smart homes identify and differentiate an elderly individual from others present in the home environment?

query.text: How do health smart homes identify and differentiate an elderly individual from others present in the home environment?
query.answer: Health smart homes usually <cite id="a15c3582-1">differentiate people by attaching identity to signals from body-worn tags such as RFID, UWB, Wi‑Fi, or BLE, which provide information about the relative location of multiple individuals in the home</cite>. In fact, <cite id="a15c3582-0">one reviewed system “can track and identify each resident wearing a BLE tag”</cite>, and <cite id="a15c3582-0">reported 96% accuracy</cite>. When wearables are undesirable, some systems use <cite id="a15c3582-4">non-wearable identification through ambient non-intrusive UWB sensors</cite> or <cite id="c82c071d-0">“behaviometrics” to determine residents’ identities without a wireless tracking tag or biometric identifiers such as facial recognition</cite>. Other smart homes also use <cite id="a6550172-0">video-based systems that can monitor activities and recognize complex gait</cite>, so the older adult may be distinguished by movement patterns. Some systems additionally try to separate the target elder from nonresidents by <cite id="c82c071d-1">detecting the presence of visitors in the home using only wireless motion-sensor data</cite>. Overall, identification is done by combining identity-linked wearables, location sensing, and sometimes behavior/gait analysis, though <cite id="a15c3582-5">the clinical utility of localization remains mixed</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do the configuration and positioning of thermal sensors affect the accuracy and directional sensitivity of blood velocity measurements?

query.text: How do the configuration and positioning of thermal sensors affect the accuracy and directional sensitivity of blood velocity measurements?
query.answer:
Thermal-sensor <cite id="43efcc10-1">configuration strongly affects directional sensitivity: although thermal anemometer flow sensors can measure a wide range of flow velocity, it is difficult to determine flow direction through a single heater.</cite> In contrast, <cite id="55aa6f69-4">devices that measure temperature differences between upstream and downstream thermistors</cite> gain directional information because <cite id="43efcc10-4">more heat is transferred to the downstream temperature sensors than to the upstream temperature sensors</cite>; correspondingly, <cite id="43efcc10-5">the downstream sensor will be hotter than the upstream sensor.</cite> This differential layout also improves accuracy, since <cite id="ecdc0396-0">ΔT between the upstream and downstream thermistors can accurately reflect heat convection while cancelling out ambient thermal influence.</cite>

Sensor <cite id="9848b31d-1">positioning also matters because converting thermal signals to blood flow rates relies on models that include a linear vessel of radius R and a distance h beneath the surface,</cite> so vessel depth and alignment relative to the vessel change the measured response. Placement can even perturb the measurement itself: <cite id="9848b31d-2">pressure applied directly above the vessel reduces the measured blood flow, while application away from the vessel</cite> avoids that artifact. For intravascular measurements, positional awareness helps further, because <cite id="43efcc10-2">by being able to detect the position of the catheter within the flow channel, the 3-D thermal flow sensor can realize more accurate assessment of intravascular heat transfer and flow.</cite>

fully_underspecified.answer: Sensor setup and placement strongly affect both accuracy and directional sensitivity. <cite id="587d6793-4">Calibration is critical to ensuring that the output from sensors is accurate and repeatable within the specified operating conditions.</cite> For directional response, <cite id="71778fb3-1">a single-axis accelerometer only measures data in one specific direction</cite>, so <cite id="587d6793-1">aligning the sensor axes with the reference frame—for example, sensor X forward and Z down in a vehicle installation</cite> helps ensure the sensor measures the intended component of motion. query.text: What are the common practices and challenges involved in validating ovarian follicle detection methods using human ultrasound imaging data?
query.answer:
Common validation practice is to <cite id="e9d00257-0">test algorithms on shared, annotated ultrasound datasets</cite>, because <cite id="e9d00257-0">“an objective comparison of different follicle-detection approaches is only possible when all are tested on the same data.”</cite> A notable example is USOVA3D, <cite id="e9d00257-0">“the first publicly accessible … database of annotated ultrasound volumes with ovarian follicles,”</cite> created specifically for this purpose. In that dataset, <cite id="e9d00257-0">“the ovary and all follicles were annotated in each volume by two medical experts,”</cite> and it includes <cite id="e9d00257-0">“a general verification protocol for unbiased assessment of detection algorithms that can be compared and ranked by scoring according to this protocol.”</cite>

Another common practice is to validate against expert human readings from clinical ultrasound. In a recent multicenter IVF study, <cite id="b1b80e19-0">performance was evaluated “compared to assessments by certified sonographers”</cite> using <cite id="b1b80e19-0">5508 transvaginal ultrasound scans from 1689 patients across four IVF centers</cite>. The study used <cite id="b1b80e19-0">training/validation data, an independent test set, and a consensus test set annotated by three expert sonographers</cite>, which is a strong validation design for assessing generalization and reader agreement.

Typical evaluation metrics include detection and segmentation accuracy measures. For detection/counting studies, <cite id="b1b80e19-0">“model performance was assessed using precision, recall, and F1 score.”</cite> For segmentation studies, common metrics include <cite id="06d8b543-0">mAP, IOU, and Dice score</cite>. Validation may also assess workflow impact, such as labeling time, since <cite id="b1b80e19-0">annotation efficiency was measured by comparing manual and AI-assisted times</cite>.

The main challenges are:

- <cite id="06d8b543-0">Pixel-level annotations for fully supervised segmentation are “often impractical due to time and workload constraints.”</cite>
- <cite id="06d8b543-0">There is “annotation scarcity,”</cite> so studies may rely on weaker labels such as bounding boxes rather than full masks.
- <cite id="06d8b543-0">Follicles have “diverse sizes and shapes,”</cite> which makes robust detection and segmentation harder.
- <cite id="e9d00257-0">Automated follicle detection in ovarian ultrasound volumes “remains a challenging task,”</cite> and even expert reference labels are not perfectly consistent: <cite id="e9d00257-0">the USOVA3D testing set showed intra-rater overall score of around 83/100</cite>, indicating meaningful annotation variability.
- Public data remain limited; the weakly supervised study explicitly says its new dataset was introduced to <cite id="06d8b543-0">“address[] the scarcity in reproductive health data.”</cite>

So, in short: validation usually relies on expert-annotated human ultrasound datasets, held-out or multicenter test sets, consensus reads, and metrics such as precision/recall/F1 or IoU/Dice; the hardest parts are limited public datasets, costly manual annotation, inter-expert variability, and the visual complexity of follicles in ultrasound.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the common practices and challenges involved in validating detection methods using imaging data?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Common validation practices for detection methods using imaging data usually include:

- <cite id="14b84b9e-0">using cross-validation during model development</cite>, especially when datasets are limited.
- <cite id="14b84b9e-2">reporting task-appropriate evaluation metrics</cite> rather than relying on a single score.
- <cite id="cbfe9f3b-5">testing on external data that were not used in development</cite> to assess whether performance holds beyond the original dataset.
- <cite id="1032dbec-9">checking observer variability by having multiple annotators label representative cases and measuring agreement</cite>, because the reference labels themselves may be uncertain.
- <cite id="1032dbec-5">carefully defining labeling instructions</cite> since annotation protocols affect annotation quality.

The main challenges are:

- <cite id="cbfe9f3b-0">data scarcity, imbalance, privacy, and domain shift</cite>, all of which make reliable validation harder.
- <cite id="1032dbec-1">cross-population domain shift can change model performance across settings</cite>, so results from one site or population may not generalize.
- <cite id="cbfe9f3b-1">bias in medical imaging datasets and models</cite>, which can distort apparent performance for some groups.
- <cite id="1032dbec-0">interobserver variability reflects differences in reliability and measurement error</cite>, making the “ground truth” less definitive.
- <cite id="1032dbec-5">annotation quality depends on the labeling instructions used</cite>, and <cite id="1032dbec-7">annotation biases can affect conventional notions of generalization</cite>.
- <cite id="cbfe9f3b-5">many imaging AI algorithms perform unimpressively on external validation</cite>, highlighting overfitting to development data.

In short: good practice is to validate with rigorous splits, appropriate metrics, external datasets, and label-quality checks; the biggest difficulties are limited and biased data, imperfect annotations, and poor generalization across scanners, sites, and populations. <cite id="14b84b9e-0">Cross-validation is widely used in medical imaging AI development</cite>, but <cite id="cbfe9f3b-5">external validation is crucial because performance often drops on independent data</cite>.

without_term.text: How are costing methods for disease testing services in a region of Africa classified, and what are the key distinctions that define each classification?
without_term.answer:
Costing methods used for disease testing services in African settings are usually classified along <cite id="14833c78-3">two key dimensions: bottom-up versus top-down, and micro-costing versus gross-costing.</cite> A general framework paper found that the common combinations are <cite id="14833c78-5">top-down micro-costing, top-down gross-costing, and bottom-up micro-costing.</cite>

The key distinctions are:

1. **Top-down vs. bottom-up**
   - **Top-down costing** starts with total expenditure or budget data and then allocates those costs to a service, department, or test output. <cite id="14833c78-0">The top-down approach relies on comprehensive program or facility costs</cite> and <cite id="14833c78-2">allocates the total budget (expenditures) to a particular department or service.</cite>
   - **Bottom-up costing** identifies the individual resources used for each service/test and sums them. <cite id="14833c78-2">Bottom-up costing quantifies and costs every input consumed</cite> and is based on <cite id="14833c78-6">each input of the intervention.</cite>

2. **Micro-costing vs. gross-costing**
   - **Micro-costing** measures resources in detailed, disaggregated units. <cite id="14833c78-7">Micro-costing studies collect detailed data on resources utilized and the value of those resources.</cite>
   - **Gross-costing** uses broader, more aggregated averages or lump-sum estimates instead of itemizing each component. <cite id="14833c78-8">Gross costing (top-down costing) and micro-costing (bottom-up costing) are not mutually exclusive methods, but can be seen as two ends of the costing spectrum.</cite>

So, in practice for disease testing services in sub-Saharan Africa, the classifications are defined by:
- whether costs are derived from **aggregate spending** or **itemized resource use**, and
- whether measurement is **highly detailed** or **more aggregated**.  

That is why studies are often described as:
- **Top-down gross-costing**: allocate total program/lab spending using broad averages;
- **Top-down micro-costing**: start from facility/program totals but disaggregate and allocate to specific testing activities in more detail;
- **Bottom-up micro-costing**: measure each input used per test or per patient and sum them. <cite id="14833c78-5">These are the most commonly observed classifications in the literature.</cite>

For context, this framework is directly relevant to testing-service evidence from the region: a systematic review of <cite id="b259b6f0-0">HIV testing services costs in sub-Saharan Africa</cite> synthesized cost estimates across many studies in the region, where such methodological differences help explain variation in reported costs.

questions.original_query: How do mobile genetic elements influence the genetic diversity and host specificity of bovine Staphylococcus aureus strains?

query.text: How do mobile genetic elements influence the genetic diversity and host specificity of bovine Staphylococcus aureus strains?
query.answer: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) strongly shape both the adaptation process and the movement of DNA among and within bacterial populations in S. aureus. More broadly, S. aureus can adapt rapidly to different hosts mainly through the acquisition of mobile genetic elements (MGEs). For bovine S. aureus, the key influence of MGEs is on host adaptation after host jumps. In ruminant-associated lineages, bovine mastitis strains evolved from a human ancestor after a host jump, and this transition was linked to the acquisition of a novel mobile genetic element encoding a variant von Willebrand factor-binding protein (vWbpSaa1) together with the loss of the human-specific immune evasion cluster (IEC) genes. Consistently, another comparative study found that a phiSa3-like prophage carrying the immune evasion cluster genes was identified in human isolates but not in animal isolates, while a pathogenicity island carrying a variant von Willebrand factor-binding protein was found in all isolates of a bovine-specific clone. This indicates that host specificity is influenced both by gaining ruminant-beneficial MGEs and by losing human-adapted MGEs. MGEs also contribute to genetic diversity among bovine strains by differentiating lineages in virulence content and disease behavior. In bovine mastitis isolates, distinct lineages differ by variants in virulence-related genes and mobile genetic elements, and these differences are associated with distinct within-host responses and clinical outcomes. Likewise, comparative genomics showed that distinct lineages were associated with clinical and subclinical mastitis, and isolates associated with clinical mastitis harbored more virulence genes. This suggests MGEs expand or reshuffle the accessory genome, helping generate strain-to-strain diversity in pathogenic potential. Specific pathogenicity islands appear especially important. Evidence from ruminant adaptation studies shows that acquisition of a novel staphylococcal pathogenicity island played a role in bovine host adaptation, while in sheep and goats acquisition of a novel staphylococcal pathogenicity island (SaPIov2) caused a host switch from humans to small ruminants. Newer work on bovine strains also identified a novel bovine-specific adhesin carried on a pathogenicity island, SAPIbov1, predicted to mediate host-specific colonization. Together, these findings support a model in which MGEs provide host-matched adhesins, coagulation/colonization factors, and immune-evasion functions that improve survival in the bovine mammary gland. In short: bovine S. aureus diversity and host specificity are driven in large part by MGE turnover. Acquisition of bovine-adaptive elements, loss of human-specific prophage/IEC genes, and lineage-specific differences in mobile elements collectively create genetically distinct bovine strains with different capacities for colonization, immune interaction, and mastitis severity.

fully_underspecified.text: How do mobile genetic elements influence genetic diversity and host specificity of bacterial strains?
fully_underspecified.answer:
## How mobile genetic elements shape bacterial diversity

<cite id="cff8f011-1,ad326b58-0">Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are major drivers of bacterial evolution because they are crucial for horizontal gene transfer and facilitate rapid evolution and adaptation.</cite> <cite id="cce9bbb2-7">They increase genetic diversity by potentiating gene gain and loss</cite> and <cite id="cce9bbb2-2,cce9bbb2-0">by creating genome plasticity through insertion-sequence activity that affects genome evolution and adaptability.</cite> <cite id="ad326b58-2,154fef7c-4">Because MGEs often carry accessory genes such as virulence and antimicrobial-resistance determinants, they can quickly add new traits that improve host fitness and ecological performance.</cite>

<cite id="9f08629a-6">This diversification can spread widely because some mobilizable plasmids have a very broad host range</cite>, while <cite id="154fef7c-6">MGEs disseminate genes when they mobilize into new bacterial hosts.</cite> <cite id="154fef7c-8,cff8f011-0">As a result, MGEs help generate strain-to-strain differences in traits that affect host and ecosystem health.</cite>

## How mobile genetic elements influence host specificity

<cite id="9f08629a-0">A key way MGEs affect host specificity is by moving pathogenicity islands, which play a pivotal role in bacterial virulence.</cite> <cite id="9f08629a-1">Genes encoding toxins and other virulence factors can reside on pathogenicity islands as well as on plasmids, transposons, and other mobilizable elements.</cite> Since <cite id="5689c8ac-0">virulence genes encode functions needed for host infection, colonization, tissue invasion, and immune evasion,</cite> <cite id="ad326b58-2,5689c8ac-1">acquiring or losing MGE-borne virulence genes can alter bacterial adaptability, fitness, and pathogenicity, thereby changing which hosts or tissues a strain can successfully exploit.</cite>

<cite id="9f08629a-6">MGE host range also matters: some elements transfer broadly, whereas transfer in general depends on reaching susceptible hosts.</cite> That means <cite id="9f08629a-6,154fef7c-6">the host range of the mobile element itself helps determine which bacterial lineages can receive host-adaptation genes, indirectly shaping the emergence of host-specific strains.</cite>

## Bottom line

<cite id="cff8f011-1,cce9bbb2-7,cce9bbb2-2">MGEs influence genetic diversity by moving DNA between bacteria, driving gene gain/loss, and remodeling genomes.</cite> <cite id="9f08629a-0,9f08629a-1,5689c8ac-0">They influence host specificity when the transferred DNA encodes host-interaction functions—especially virulence, colonization, and immune-evasion factors—so that strains acquire or lose the capacity to thrive in particular hosts.</cite>

without_scope.text: How do mobile genetic elements influence the genetic diversity and host specificity of Staphylococcus aureus strains?
without_scope.answer:
### Mobile genetic elements as the main source of strain-to-strain variation

<cite id="c8469cfc-1,e469399b-3">In *Staphylococcus aureus*, rapid adaptation and much of the organism’s genomic plasticity are driven by mobile genetic elements (MGEs), especially prophages, plasmids, and pathogenicity islands.</cite> <cite id="c8469cfc-4">Its genome carries heterogeneous MGEs, including insertion sequences, transposons, and transposon-like elements.</cite> <cite id="c8469cfc-3">Across isolates, genetic diversity correlates with distinct acquisitions of SCCmec elements, antibiotic-resistance genes, virulence genes, and other mobile elements.</cite>

### How MGEs generate genetic diversity

<cite id="4abaa096-0">A clear example is SCCmec: all MRSA strains contain SCCmec, which encodes *mecA* and confers resistance to methicillin and all β-lactam antibiotics.</cite> <cite id="e469399b-2,e469399b-6">Another major class is the staphylococcal pathogenicity islands (SaPIs), which are MGEs that encode virulence factors, including superantigen and other virulence determinants, and depend on helper phages for mobilization.</cite> <cite id="6bbf86a0-0">Temperate phages add still more variation, because *S. aureus* strains can carry up to four temperate phages, many of which possess accessory genes encoding staphylococcal virulence factors.</cite> <cite id="e469399b-9">Phages and PICIs can also mediate intra- and inter-species plasmid transfer, providing another route for horizontal gene flow.</cite>

### How MGEs shape host specificity

<cite id="c8469cfc-6">Genomic and epidemiological studies show that *S. aureus* has jumped between host species many times over its evolutionary history, and these jumps have involved the acquisition and loss of mobile genetic elements.</cite> <cite id="6bbf86a0-3,d4895214-7">A particularly important host-specific module is the immune evasion cluster on β-hemolysin-converting bacteriophages: its virulence factors are highly human specific, and these human-specific immune evasion proteins contribute to human niche adaptation.</cite> <cite id="d4895214-2">Consistent with that, livestock-associated MRSA can acquire phage-encoded immune modulators such as the immune evasion cluster.</cite> <cite id="d4895214-0">More broadly, prophage-encoded immune evasion factors are critical for *S. aureus* host transmissibility, infection, switching, and adaptation.</cite>

### Bottom line

<cite id="c8469cfc-1,c8469cfc-6,c8469cfc-3,d4895214-0">So, MGEs influence *S. aureus* in two linked ways: they diversify strains by moving resistance and virulence genes between genomes, and they alter host specificity by adding or removing host-adaptive traits that help lineages colonize, transmit in, or switch between particular animal hosts.</cite>

without_term.text: How do mobile genetic elements influence the genetic diversity and host specificity of bacterial strains?
without_term.answer:
Mobile genetic elements increase bacterial genetic diversity mainly by <cite id="d41f34f0-0">facilitat[ing] horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bacteria</cite>, which <cite id="d41f34f0-2">traffic[s] adaptive traits between species and strains</cite>. They influence host specificity because the same mobile DNA often carries the genes that determine how well a strain survives in, colonizes, or causes disease in a particular host. For example, <cite id="51acb864-5,a3a80d5c-3">pathogenicity islands play a pivotal role in the virulence of bacterial pathogens of humans and are also essential for virulence in pathogens of animals</cite>, and <cite id="c6d7fce2-3">the diversity in cargo genes across different strains is a key factor in the pathogen's ability to adapt to new hosts</cite>. In addition, some MGEs themselves can move into <cite id="a3a80d5c-1">new bacterial hosts</cite>, spreading host-adaptive genes across lineages. So, in short, MGEs shape both <cite id="d41f34f0-0,d41f34f0-2">genetic diversity through HGT</cite> and <cite id="c6d7fce2-3,51acb864-5">host specificity by moving host-interaction and virulence determinants that enable adaptation to particular hosts</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do plasmids and transposons facilitate the horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes among Listeria species and other bacteria?

query.text: How do plasmids and transposons facilitate the horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes among Listeria species and other bacteria?
query.answer: In <cite id="d141e8fb-0">Listeria monocytogenes, horizontal gene transfer mediated by mobile genetic elements—including plasmids and transposons—facilitates the exchange of antimicrobial resistance determinants</cite>. More specifically, <cite id="d141e8fb-1">antimicrobial resistance acquisition in L. monocytogenes primarily occurs through the mobilization of plasmids and integrative conjugative elements</cite>. In bacteria more broadly, <cite id="92193eee-4">many resistance plasmids are conjugative, meaning they encode the functions needed for cell-to-cell DNA transfer</cite>, and <cite id="92193eee-3">plasmids are key players in the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance by transferring resistance genes between bacteria via horizontal gene transfer</cite>. Transposons complement this by moving resistance genes between replicons: <cite id="49e93b1a-0">transposons can transfer from a plasmid to other plasmids or from a DNA chromosome to plasmid and vice versa</cite>, and <cite id="49e93b1a-1">conjugative transposons have a surprisingly broad host range and probably contribute as much as plasmids to the spread of antibiotic resistance genes</cite>. In Listeria, this is seen in concrete examples such as <cite id="24bdcffc-1">a food isolate in which tetracycline resistance was associated with the tetM gene in plasmid DNA</cite> and <cite id="3bcf83f4-1">Tn6198, a transposon in L. monocytogenes in which the trimethoprim resistance gene dfrG is embedded into a Tn916 element</cite>. Together, these elements let resistance genes be <cite id="24bdcffc-5">moved between distantly related taxa</cite> by using plasmids as transferable vehicles and transposons as mobile “cut-and-paste” or “copy-and-paste” modules that insert resistance genes into plasmids or chromosomes, making onward spread possible across Listeria species and other bacteria <cite id="49e93b1a-0,92193eee-4">.</cite>

without_scope.text: How do plasmids and transposons facilitate the horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes among bacteria?
without_scope.answer: <cite id="e8c29fdb-0">Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) plays an important role in bacterial evolution and greatly facilitates the rapid spread of resistance genes</cite>. <cite id="b4debeab-3">The widespread prevalence of AMR is, in part, due to the horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), typically mediated by plasmids</cite>. <cite id="b4debeab-1">Conjugative plasmids are able to promote their own transfer and the transfer of other plasmids from one bacterial cell to another</cite>, and <cite id="e8c29fdb-6">this form of HGT, known as conjugation, perpetuates the spread of plasmids across bacterial populations</cite>. <cite id="b4debeab-4">Transposons are mobile genetic elements able to move within or between DNA molecules</cite>; specifically, <cite id="fe9982e9-0">transposase- or recombinase-catalyzed reactions can transfer ARGs from plasmids to chromosomes and vice versa</cite>, and <cite id="fe9982e9-4">transposons can also move from a plasmid to other plasmids</cite>. So, plasmids mainly <cite id="b4debeab-1,e8c29fdb-6">spread resistance genes between bacterial cells by conjugation</cite>, while transposons <cite id="fe9982e9-0,fe9982e9-4">capture and reshuffle those genes between plasmids and chromosomes</cite>, making it easier for resistance determinants to accumulate and disseminate.

without_term.text: How do mobile genetic elements facilitate the horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes among bacteria?
without_term.answer: Mobile genetic elements facilitate the horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes by acting as <cite id="15c0e45f-1">central to horizontal gene transfer (HGT), serving microbes by trafficking adaptive traits between species and strains</cite>. The main route is often via plasmids: <cite id="61e1348b-1">Plasmids are ubiquitous vectors for HGT and often carry a variety of antimicrobial resistance genes</cite>, and during conjugation <cite id="61e1348b-5">two bacteria can pair up and connect through structures in the cell membranes and then transfer DNA from one bacterial cell to another</cite>. Other elements then load and rearrange resistance genes on those plasmids. <cite id="7443631d-4">Insertion sequences (IS) and transposons (Tn) are discrete DNA segments that are able to move themselves (and associated resistance genes)</cite>, so they can shift resistance genes between chromosomes and plasmids; in addition, <cite id="7443631d-3">transposition of IS elements or transposons can promote antibiotic resistance by changing bacterial gene expression</cite>. Integrons further accelerate this process because <cite id="61e1348b-0">transposons capture integron gene cassettes to yield high mobility integrons that target res sites of plasmids</cite>, and <cite id="61e1348b-0">these plasmids, in turn</cite> disseminate those cassettes through bacterial populations. Beyond plasmids, <cite id="15c0e45f-9">integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) are widespread mobile DNA that transmit both vertically, in a host-integrated state, and horizontally</cite>, and <cite id="7443631d-0">MGEs such as plasmids, transposons, integrons and bacteriophages are the part of bacterial mobilome through which genetic exchange takes place</cite>. In short, MGEs spread antimicrobial resistance by <cite id="61e1348b-1,61e1348b-5">carrying resistance genes</cite>, <cite id="7443631d-4">moving them between DNA locations</cite>, <cite id="61e1348b-0">capturing them into gene-cassette systems</cite>, and <cite id="61e1348b-5,15c0e45f-9">transferring them between bacterial cells</cite>.

questions.original_query: How does the vaginal microbiota composition differ between healthy women and those diagnosed with cervical dysplasia?

query.text: How does the vaginal microbiota composition differ between healthy women and those diagnosed with cervical dysplasia?
query.answer:
In general, the vaginal microbiota of healthy women is <cite id="c0d06839-0">Lactobacillus-dominant</cite>, and <cite id="c0d06839-5">healthy women predominantly exhibited CST I, with Lactobacillus crispatus as the dominant microorganism.</cite>

By contrast, women diagnosed with cervical dysplasia tend to show a shift away from this protective pattern: <cite id="c0d06839-1">women with cervical dysplasia had increased vaginal microbiota diversity</cite> and <cite id="c0d06839-1">differentially abundant taxa</cite>. Across studies, <cite id="c0d06839-3">18 out of 23 studies reported a significant decrease in Lactobacillus species in the cervical, cervicovaginal, and vaginal samples</cite>. Dysplasia is also associated with <cite id="c0d06839-5">CST IV</cite>, and <cite id="c0d06839-4">the diversity of VMB increased with advancing cervical dysplasia severity</cite> while <cite id="c0d06839-4">an anaerobic VMB is associated</cite> with disease.

So, briefly: healthy women usually have a low-diversity, Lactobacillus-rich vaginal microbiota, whereas cervical dysplasia is more often associated with reduced Lactobacillus dominance, greater microbial diversity, and enrichment of anaerobic/CST IV-type communities.

questions.original_query: How can respiratory physiotherapists use diaphragm ultrasonography to support the weaning process in mechanically ventilated patients?

query.text: How can respiratory physiotherapists use diaphragm ultrasonography to support the weaning process in mechanically ventilated patients?
query.answer:
Respiratory physiotherapists can use diaphragm ultrasonography as a <cite id="446d7b48-0">bedside assessment of diaphragm thickness/thickening fraction (TFdi) and diaphragm motion/excursion</cite> to add objective information about inspiratory muscle function during weaning from mechanical ventilation.

A practical approach is:

1. **Measure the key diaphragm ultrasound variables**
   - In the **zone of apposition**, assess diaphragm thickness and calculate TFdi. <cite id="446d7b48-0">TFdi = (end-inspiratory thickness − end-expiratory thickness)/end-expiratory thickness × 100%</cite>
   - In the **subcostal view**, assess diaphragm excursion with M-mode. <cite id="446d7b48-0">Diaphragm motion can be measured using M-mode US in the subcostal view.</cite>

2. **Use TFdi as a marker of inspiratory effort/readiness**
   - Diaphragm ultrasound provides information on <cite id="df83bf44-0">thickness (diaphragm thickening fraction [TFdi]) and movement or excursion</cite>.
   - TFdi appears to reflect diaphragm effort, because <cite id="446d7b48-0">changes in diaphragmatic thickness correlated with inspiratory effort measured by transdiaphragmatic pressure</cite> and <cite id="446d7b48-0">thickening fraction correlated with diaphragmatic pressure-time product in pressure support ventilation</cite>.
   - During/around a spontaneous breathing trial, a higher TFdi may support extubation readiness: <cite id="446d7b48-0">Ferrari et al. identified a thickening fraction over 36% as an index of successful extubation after a spontaneous breathing trial, with sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 88%</cite>. Another study also found <cite id="df83bf44-1">a higher diaphragmatic thickening fraction was significantly associated with successful extubation</cite>.

3. **Identify possible diaphragmatic dysfunction that may explain weaning difficulty**
   - Very low values may indicate risk: <cite id="df83bf44-8">weaning failure was associated with diaphragmatic excursion <1 cm and thickening fraction <28%</cite>.
   - This can help physiotherapists recognize patients who may need closer monitoring, inspiratory muscle loading optimization, secretion management, positioning, or delayed extubation planning rather than relying only on conventional indices.

4. **Integrate ultrasound with the wider clinical picture**
   - Diaphragm ultrasound should support, not replace, standard weaning assessment. A recent review found <cite id="446d7b48-0">an integrated ultrasonographic evaluation of the heart, lungs, diaphragm, and expiratory muscles can enhance decision making in the weaning process</cite>.
   - At the same time, evidence is mixed: <cite id="446d7b48-0">a multicenter study reported poor accuracy of diaphragmatic excursion and thickening fraction for predicting weaning failure within 48 h</cite>, and overall <cite id="446d7b48-0">the utility of diaphragm US in routine weaning assessment remains uncertain due to methodological heterogeneity and inconsistent evidence</cite>.

5. **Be cautious when interpreting excursion**
   - Excursion is useful, but <cite id="446d7b48-0">in mechanically ventilated patients it can be influenced by accessory muscle activity or passive displacement by the ventilator</cite>, so physiotherapists should avoid overinterpreting excursion alone.

**In summary:** respiratory physiotherapists can use diaphragm ultrasonography to quantify diaphragm contractile activity and motion during weaning, especially by tracking TFdi and excursion before or during SBTs. It is most useful as an adjunct to clinical assessment and other weaning markers to detect diaphragmatic dysfunction, gauge respiratory muscle performance, and support extubation decisions. <cite id="446d7b48-0">Diaphragm US can provide valuable insights into respiratory muscle function of ICU patients, aiding optimization of ventilatory support and identification of diaphragmatic dysfunction.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: How can healthcare professionals use ultrasound to support the process in patients on mechanical ventilation?
fully_underspecified.answer: In mechanically ventilated patients, healthcare professionals can use <cite id="S26,S28">ultrasound during the process of liberation from mechanical ventilation, including weaning and extubation</cite>. A multimodal point-of-care ultrasound exam can assess <cite id="S26">upper airway patency, pulmonary aeration, diaphragmatic function, cardiac function, and venous congestion</cite>, with lung ultrasound helping detect <cite id="S34,S36">B-lines, consolidations, pleural effusions, and other signs of loss of aeration or pulmonary edema that may predict post-extubation distress or failure</cite>. Diaphragm ultrasound can measure <cite id="S37">diaphragmatic excursion and thickening fraction</cite> to evaluate <cite id="S38,S39">diaphragmatic dysfunction and higher risk of extubation failure</cite>, while cardiac ultrasound can identify <cite id="S40,S42">high left ventricular filling pressure and weaning-induced pulmonary edema, allowing tailored treatment</cite>. As an adjunct to standard extubation protocols, ultrasound can <cite id="S43,S45">identify clinically occult causes of failure, improve risk stratification, and guide optimization before extubation</cite>.

without_scope.text: How can respiratory physiotherapists use diaphragm ultrasonography to support the weaning process in patients?
without_scope.answer:
Respiratory physiotherapists can use diaphragm ultrasonography as a <cite id="f25c8b4e-0">bedside assessment of diaphragm thickness (especially thickening fraction, TFdi) and movement/excursion to detect diaphragmatic dysfunction</cite>, which matters because <cite id="f25c8b4e-0">a frequent cause of weaning and extubation failure in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients is diaphragm muscle dysfunction</cite>.

In practice, it can support weaning in 4 main ways:

1. **Identify patients at risk of weaning/extubation failure**
   - <cite id="f25c8b4e-0">Diaphragmatic dynamics and thickness parameters together assessed by ultrasonography could predict the success of extubation</cite>.
   - Commonly used indicators are <cite id="cf17f7df-1">diaphragmatic thickening fraction (dTF) and diaphragmatic excursion (DE)</cite>.
   - Reported thresholds in the literature include <cite id="447fabb4-0">diaphragmatic excursion cut-off values of 10 mm to 13 mm or more</cite> and <cite id="cf17f7df-8">diaphragmatic thickening measurements ... with optimal cutoffs ranging from 30% to 36%</cite>.

2. **Add objective information before or during a spontaneous breathing trial**
   - Physiotherapists can measure excursion and thickening during tidal or spontaneous breathing to judge whether diaphragm recruitment appears adequate, since <cite id="f25c8b4e-0">the ultrasonographic analysis of excursion of the diaphragm, inspiratory and expiratory thickness, and TFdi (>20%) allow in its set and with normal values, predict success or failure for the extubation</cite>.

3. **Track response to rehabilitation and ventilator unloading**
   - Serial scans can be used to monitor whether diaphragm function is improving or worsening over time, because <cite id="f25c8b4e-0">US evaluation of the diaphragm yields important data regarding its thickness ... and its movement or excursion</cite>. This can help physiotherapists time progression of mobilization, breathing exercises, and weaning steps.

4. **Integrate findings with the wider weaning assessment**
   - Diaphragm ultrasound should not be used alone. Evidence suggests value when combined with other bedside assessments: <cite id="92e14dc4-0">employing an inclusive ultrasound protocol incorporating lung, diaphragm, and cardiac sonography reliably predicted the likelihood</cite> of weaning success.
   - Also, caution is needed because results are not uniformly strong across studies; for example, <cite id="cf17f7df-2">approximately 50% of patients had low diaphragm excursion (< 10 mm) and around 70% had weak diaphragm thickening (< 30%)</cite>, and that study questioned predictive performance.

**Practical takeaway:** respiratory physiotherapists can use diaphragm ultrasonography to <cite id="cf17f7df-3">aid in predicting extubation success by monitoring diaphragm morphology through parameters such as diaphragm thickness [and] diaphragmatic excursion</cite>, mainly as an adjunct to clinical examination, spontaneous breathing trial performance, cough/airway clearance, gas exchange, and broader lung/cardiac ultrasound findings.

So, the best use is as an **objective adjunct**: measure **excursion** and **thickening fraction**, repeat them over time, and use the results to help decide whether a patient is ready to progress in weaning or may need more respiratory muscle support/training before extubation.

questions.original_query: How does the presentation and recognition of lung involvement in CMV pneumonia differ between immunocompromised and immunocompetent critically ill patients?

query.text: How does the presentation and recognition of lung involvement in CMV pneumonia differ between immunocompromised and immunocompetent critically ill patients?
query.answer:
In broad terms, CMV lung disease is **classically expected and therefore more readily considered in immunocompromised patients**, whereas in **immunocompetent critically ill patients** it is usually **reactivation during ICU illness**, is **less expected**, and is therefore **harder to recognize because the presentation is nonspecific**.

- In **immunocompromised patients**, CMV is a well-known opportunistic pulmonary pathogen: <cite id="87ba479b-0">CMV infection is a known opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients</cite>. Lung involvement is often approached as a recognized cause of severe pneumonia in this group, and diagnosis commonly relies on respiratory sampling: <cite id="fa9b0fc3-1">CMV pneumonia can be diagnosed by detecting the virus in serum and/or respiratory samples such as bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or tracheal</cite>; <cite id="fa9b0fc3-5">CMV immunostaining in the BAL fluid is a very helpful method to diagnose CMV pneumonitis in these patients.</cite> Typical presentation includes <cite id="a7c47a1c-3">fever and shortness of breath, accompanied by an interstitial infiltrate</cite>.

- In **immunocompetent critically ill patients**, CMV is increasingly recognized as part of ICU-associated immunoparesis rather than pre-existing immune suppression: <cite id="87ba479b-0">sepsis, high disease severity, prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stay and medications with immunosuppressive effects... can cause immunoparesis, even in patients with no previous history of immunosuppression</cite>. In this population, recognition is more difficult because <cite id="a7c47a1c-0">CMV presents with non-specific symptoms, affecting multiple organs making it difficult to suspect and identify in critically ill patients.</cite> The diagnosis may be delayed or overlooked since <cite id="87ba479b-0">the diagnosis of CMV infection may be challenging in such patients due to non-specific symptoms and multiorgan involvement</cite>. Its burden is also not trivial: <cite id="325fcdff-0">a systematic review of 13 studies with 1258 critically ill immunocompetent patients showed the rate of active CMV infection to be 17%</cite>.

So the key difference is:

1. **Presentation**
   - **Immunocompromised:** CMV pneumonia is a familiar opportunistic pneumonia, often presenting as viral pneumonitis with fever, dyspnea, and interstitial infiltrates. <cite id="a7c47a1c-3">The most common clinical presentation of CMV pneumonia is fever and shortness of breath, accompanied by an interstitial infiltrate.</cite>
   - **Immunocompetent critically ill:** pulmonary involvement is more likely to be embedded in a broader ICU syndrome with sepsis/multiorgan dysfunction and nonspecific respiratory findings, rather than a clearly suspected primary CMV pneumonia. <cite id="a7c47a1c-0">CMV presents with non-specific symptoms, affecting multiple organs</cite>

2. **Recognition**
   - **Immunocompromised:** clinicians usually have a lower threshold to test for CMV, often using BAL and related virologic/pathologic methods. <cite id="fa9b0fc3-1,fa9b0fc3-5">CMV pneumonia can be diagnosed... in serum and/or respiratory samples such as BAL... CMV immunostaining in the BAL fluid is a very helpful method</cite>
   - **Immunocompetent critically ill:** clinicians may not initially suspect CMV; recognition requires a higher index of suspicion because findings are nonspecific and can mimic other ICU pneumonias. <cite id="a7c47a1c-1">The diagnosis of CMV pneumonia can be challenging as it may present with nonspecific clinical and radiological features</cite> <cite id="87ba479b-0">the need for treatment and therapeutic approaches in immunocompetent critically ill patients is still ambiguous</cite>

In one sentence: **CMV lung involvement in immunocompromised patients is usually a recognized opportunistic pneumonia that is actively sought, whereas in immunocompetent critically ill patients it is more often an under-recognized ICU reactivation syndrome with nonspecific pulmonary and systemic features.**

questions.original_query: How do baseline periodontal conditions and patient age affect healing outcomes after third molar surgery?

query.text: How do baseline periodontal conditions and patient age affect healing outcomes after third molar surgery?
query.answer:
Baseline periodontal condition and age both matter, but in different ways.

- In general, periodontal measures around the adjacent second molar tend to improve after impacted mandibular third molar removal: <cite id="4bd25e28-0">PI, GI, BOP, PD, and EA–OS were significantly reduced after 1, 3, and 6 months compared to baseline data</cite>, and <cite id="4bd25e28-0">there was a significant improvement of periodontal conditions of the second molar and adjacent sextant after impacted third molar surgery</cite>.

- However, worse baseline periodontal status predicts worse healing outcomes. In a 2023 study comparing periodontally susceptible versus healthy patients, <cite id="a24d7c29-0">the PSP group was 6.43 times more likely to have PPD ≥ 5 mm at T1</cite>. Also, <cite id="a24d7c29-0">every 1% increase in full mouth bleeding score at T1 was associated with 2.64mm less bone gain at M2</cite>. The authors concluded that <cite id="a24d7c29-0">second molars in patients with higher gingival inflammation were associated with less bone gain</cite>. So, patients starting with more inflammation or periodontal susceptibility are more likely to have residual pockets and less favorable bone healing.

- Age also affects healing. Evidence summarized in a clinical appraisal states that <cite id="638d0113-7">periodontal healing after impacted lower 3rd molar surgery was impaired in individuals over 30 years</cite>. The same source suggests <cite id="638d0113-7">early removal of impacted lower 3rd molars with large ...</cite> periodontal defects is beneficial, implying younger patients heal more predictably.

- By contrast, in younger adults outcomes are generally favorable: one recent review/article notes <cite id="76ede7e5-3">avulsion of impacted third molar in healthy young adults does not impair the periodontal health of adjacent second molars</cite>, and a prospective study in patients with <cite id="4bd25e28-0">Mean age: 21.89 ± 2.74</cite> found postoperative periodontal improvement.

In short: <cite id="a24d7c29-0">higher baseline inflammation/periodontal susceptibility is linked to more residual pocketing and less bone gain</cite>, while <cite id="638d0113-7">older age—especially over 30—is associated with poorer periodontal healing</cite>. Younger, periodontally healthy patients usually show the best recovery after third molar surgery.

questions.original_query: How do immunosuppressive therapy, medications, and oral hygiene together affect the development of periodontal disease in patients after liver transplantation?

query.text: How do immunosuppressive therapy, medications, and oral hygiene together affect the development of periodontal disease in patients after liver transplantation?
query.answer:
After liver transplantation, periodontal disease risk is shaped by the interaction of three factors:

1. **Immunosuppressive therapy changes the oral environment.**  
   <cite id="9d81aa01-1">Immunosuppressive medications are associated with increased risk for infection, tissue changes and cancer; they also elevate the risk for caries</cite>. This means transplant patients are more vulnerable to oral inflammation and infection while taking long-term anti-rejection drugs.

2. **The specific medication matters, especially cyclosporine vs tacrolimus.**  
   <cite id="9d81aa01-0">Cyclosporine can cause gingival hyperplasia, resulting in patient discomfort and difficulty brushing teeth, whereas tacrolimus has no adverse dental effects.</cite> Gingival enlargement can create plaque-retentive areas and make cleaning harder, which can worsen gingival inflammation and favor periodontal breakdown. Even with tacrolimus, <cite id="2a22af28-0">in renal transplant patients with poor oral hygiene and high plaque indices, gingival overgrowth has been observed in those treated with Tc</cite>, suggesting that drug effects and plaque control interact.

3. **Oral hygiene is a major modifying factor.**  
   In one transplant cohort, <cite id="d403f0d5-0">more than half (53.8%) of the liver transplant recipients had poor oral hygiene</cite>. Poor hygiene allows plaque accumulation, which amplifies inflammation and makes medication-related gingival changes more likely to become clinically important. The importance of plaque control is also reflected in the observation that <cite id="9d81aa01-6">recurrence is likely if the oral hygiene is inadequate</cite>.

Overall, these factors act **synergistically**: immunosuppression increases susceptibility to oral infection/inflammation, some drugs—especially cyclosporine—promote gingival overgrowth that makes cleaning more difficult, and inadequate oral hygiene/plaque then drives progression toward gingivitis and periodontal disease. This is clinically important because <cite id="9d81aa01-3">those patients who lacked dental treatment before LT showed an 8-fold risk for systemic infections after transplantation</cite>, and transplant experts therefore recommend <cite id="d403f0d5-0">early dental screening and pre-transplant dental treatment ... to remove any potential sources of oral infection</cite>.

**Bottom line:** In liver transplant recipients, periodontal disease tends to worsen not because of one factor alone, but because **immunosuppressive drugs increase vulnerability, certain medications (notably cyclosporine) can enlarge gingiva and hinder brushing, and poor oral hygiene/plaque then converts that vulnerability into active periodontal inflammation and disease**.

query.text: What are the typical clinical features observed in Buccal Bifurcation Cyst (BBC) cases affecting molars?
query.answer:
Typical Buccal Bifurcation Cyst (BBC) cases involving molars present as a lesion <cite id="788ad352-0">classically on the buccal surface of the mandibular first molar and less frequently the mandibular second molar.</cite> They are associated with <cite id="788ad352-1">the buccal or distobuccal aspect of the roots of partially or recently erupted teeth.</cite>

Common clinical features include:
- <cite id="788ad352-2">modest pain and swelling, and painful occlusion of teeth of the affected molar region.</cite>
- <cite id="788ad352-4">buccal swelling, delayed or incomplete eruption of teeth, and the formation of deep periodontal pockets.</cite>
- <cite id="788ad352-7">swelling, infra-occlusion, delayed eruption, localized abscess and buccal tipping of the affected molar.</cite>

So, in brief, BBC usually affects erupting mandibular first molars and typically shows buccal swelling, delayed/incomplete eruption, periodontal pocketing, pain or tenderness, occasional abscess formation, infra-occlusion, and buccal tipping of the involved molar.

questions.original_query: What are the main challenges and limitations associated with using anti-TNFα biologics in the treatment of cutaneous sarcoidosis?

query.text: What are the main challenges and limitations associated with using anti-TNFα biologics in the treatment of cutaneous sarcoidosis?
query.answer: Anti-TNFα biologics for cutaneous sarcoidosis are mainly limited by the fact that <cite id="7751d61d-0,7751d61d-8">they are generally considered third-line treatments for chronic/refractory sarcoidosis</cite> and <cite id="7751d61d-3">are usually used in combination with second-line agents</cite>. Their effectiveness in skin disease can be incomplete or delayed: <cite id="63b2ef47-2">overall cutaneous response rates were 24% at 3 months and 46% at 6 months</cite>, and although <cite id="fd991671-4">adalimumab showed better Physician Global Assessment response and reduced target lesion area versus placebo</cite>, <cite id="30cf5ea2-5">further research is still needed</cite>. Another major limitation is durability, because <cite id="fd991671-2">relapses are frequent after discontinuation</cite> and <cite id="fd991671-3">44% of patients relapsed after 18 months off treatment</cite>. Safety is also a key challenge: <cite id="63b2ef47-0,63b2ef47-5">anti-TNF therapy increases susceptibility to serious and opportunistic infections, including tuberculosis</cite>, so <cite id="30cf5ea2-4">TB screening is recommended before treatment and infliximab should be withheld during active infection</cite>; additionally, <cite id="7751d61d-2">adalimumab may increase the risk of certain cancers, autoimmune disease, and demyelinating disorders</cite>. Finally, these drugs can cause a paradoxical reaction, since <cite id="30cf5ea2-3">sarcoidosis developing during TNFα-antagonist therapy is a rare paradoxical adverse event</cite>, with <cite id="30cf5ea2-1">90 reported cases of sarcoidosis-like lesions during anti-TNF therapy</cite>, including <cite id="30cf5ea2-6">cutaneous granulomas occurring under infliximab and adalimumab</cite>.

without_term.text: What are the main challenges and limitations associated with using anti-inflammatory biologics in the treatment of skin sarcoidosis?
without_term.answer:
The main challenges and limitations of anti-inflammatory biologics for skin sarcoidosis are:

- <cite id="2315b3a7-0">their role in management is not well-defined.</cite> Most biologics are used only after standard therapies fail, because <cite id="2315b3a7-0">the accepted first-line therapy for cutaneous sarcoidosis consists of intralesional and oral corticosteroids</cite> and <cite id="2315b3a7-0">second-line agents include tetracyclines, hydroxychloroquine, and methotrexate.</cite> The available evidence mainly supports <cite id="2315b3a7-0,d47e2a42-0">infliximab and adalimumab as third-line treatments for chronic or resistant cutaneous sarcoidosis.</cite>

- The evidence base is weak. <cite id="2315b3a7-0">Although somewhat limited, the data in published studies support the use of both infliximab and adalimumab</cite>, while other biologics have only <cite id="2315b3a7-0">scattered reports</cite> and <cite id="2315b3a7-0">varying degrees of success.</cite> More broadly in sarcoidosis, there is <cite id="9ca0735d-0">lack of robust clinical trial data,</cite> so treatment has to be individualized.

- Safety is a major limitation. Anti-TNF biologics can help refractory disease but <cite id="9ca0735d-0">carry risks of serious adverse effects.</cite> Search results also note that these agents <cite id="cacdb0b7-1">increase the infection risk</cite> and <cite id="b09310d6-4">can increase the risk of infections.</cite>

- There is a paradoxical reaction problem: biologics used to treat sarcoidosis can occasionally trigger sarcoid-like disease or worsen it. <cite id="cacdb0b7-0">Drug-induced sarcoidosis-like disease is a rare side effect of anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) agents</cite>, and <cite id="b09310d6-8">some patients have experienced worsening of pre-existing</cite> sarcoidosis on anti-TNF therapy.

- Practical treatment questions remain unresolved. <cite id="2315b3a7-0">Larger and more extensive investigations are required to further assess the adverse effect profile and optimal dosing for managing cutaneous sarcoidosis.</cite> That means uncertainty about which biologic to choose, how long to treat, and how best to monitor patients.

In short: biologics can be useful for refractory skin sarcoidosis, especially anti-TNF agents, but their use is limited by <cite id="2315b3a7-0">a not well-defined role in management,</cite> <cite id="2315b3a7-0,9ca0735d-0">limited evidence,</cite> <cite id="9ca0735d-0,b09310d6-4">important safety risks,</cite> and <cite id="cacdb0b7-0,b09310d6-8">the possibility of paradoxical sarcoid-like reactions or worsening.</cite>

questions.original_query: How effective is immune checkpoint blockade in producing long-term therapeutic responses in melanoma patients?

query.text: How effective is immune checkpoint blockade in producing long-term therapeutic responses in melanoma patients?
query.answer:
Immune checkpoint blockade is <cite id="bc97c711-0">highly effective at producing durable long-term benefit in a meaningful subset of melanoma patients</cite>, but it is <cite id="ce776844-0">not universally curative</cite>.

For advanced melanoma, the strongest long-term evidence comes from the 10-year CheckMate 067 trial: <cite id="bc97c711-0">median overall survival was 71.9 months with nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 36.9 months with nivolumab alone, and 19.9 months with ipilimumab alone</cite>. The combination also showed a major reduction in risk of death versus ipilimumab, with <cite id="bc97c711-0">a hazard ratio of 0.53</cite>. Most notably for “long-term response,” <cite id="bc97c711-0">among patients who were progression-free at 3 years, 10-year melanoma-specific survival was 96% with nivolumab plus ipilimumab and 97% with nivolumab</cite>, suggesting that patients who achieve durable early disease control often maintain it for many years.

Pembrolizumab also shows durable long-term benefit: <cite id="741913cf-0">KEYNOTE-006 demonstrated significantly improved overall survival versus ipilimumab</cite>, and <cite id="22c29c8f-1">the 10-year follow-up confirms that pembrolizumab provides long-term survival benefit in advanced melanoma</cite>.

For complete responders, durability is especially strong: <cite id="ce776844-0">most complete responses were durable</cite>, though <cite id="ce776844-0">the probability of treatment failure was 27% at 3 years</cite>. So even among the best responders, relapse still occurs in a minority.

Bottom line: <cite id="bc97c711-0">immune checkpoint blockade can produce very long-lasting responses—sometimes approaching functional cure—in advanced melanoma</cite>, especially with anti–PD-1–based therapy and particularly in patients who remain progression-free for the first few years. But <cite id="ce776844-0">some patients still relapse, and many never achieve such durable control</cite>.

query.text: What are the documented remission rates for patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria in both early and longer-term follow-ups?
query.answer:
Documented remission rates for chronic spontaneous urticaria vary by follow-up length, but the literature you provided shows a clear early-versus-longer-term pattern:

- <cite id="3bfa0572-1">After 3 months, 25.2% of patients with chronic urticaria experienced remission.</cite>
- <cite id="3bfa0572-1">Approximately 50% of patients with chronic urticaria experienced remission after 11 months.</cite>
- <cite id="3bfa0572-3">The remission rates at 12 months and 36 months were 32.7% and 48.1%.</cite>
- <cite id="3bfa0572-2">Reported remission rates are 20–50% within 1 year and 45% within 5 years.</cite>
- In one prospective study, <cite id="3bfa0572-0">the cumulative prevalence of remission at 5 years was 59.1%.</cite>

So, in concise form: <cite id="3bfa0572-1,3bfa0572-3">early follow-up remission is roughly 25% at 3 months and about 33–50% by around 1 year,</cite> while <cite id="3bfa0572-2,3bfa0572-0,3bfa0572-3">longer-term remission is about 45–59% by 3–5 years.</cite>

questions.original_query: How do various probiotic treatments help reduce oxidative stress and improve skin health in models of UVB-induced photoaging?

query.text: How do various probiotic treatments help reduce oxidative stress and improve skin health in models of UVB-induced photoaging?
query.answer:
In UVB-photoaging models, probiotics appear to help mainly by <cite id="a1cf0ce7-0">reducing oxidative stress, inhibiting ECM remodeling, inhibiting the inflammatory cascade reaction, and maintaining immune homeostasis</cite>. Those upstream effects translate into better barrier function, less collagen breakdown, and improved visible skin aging markers.

Some representative examples:

- **Bifidobacterium breve strain Yakult (oral)**: in hairless mice, <cite id="00f1ed72-0">oral administration of live *Bifidobacterium breve* strain Yakult can attenuate skin barrier perturbation caused by UV and reactive oxygen species (ROS)</cite>. This suggests protection against UVB-driven oxidative injury and preservation of barrier integrity.
- **Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis MG741 (oral; fibroblasts + hairless mice)**: this probiotic <cite id="d82f16ce-0">reduces wrinkles and skin thickness by downregulating MMP-1 and MMP-3, phosphorylation of ERK, and c-FOS in fibroblasts and HR-1</cite>. It also <cite id="d82f16ce-0">inhibits the expression of NF-κB, an inflammation-related factor, in UVB-irradiated dorsal skin</cite>, helping suppress inflammatory signaling linked to photoaging. Overall, <cite id="c1dcc3cc-0">Bi. lactis MG741 has the potential to prevent wrinkles and skin inflammation by modulating skin photoaging markers</cite>.
- **Lactobacillus plantarum HY7714 (oral; fibroblasts + hairless mice)**: this strain was specifically tested <cite id="c1dcc3cc-1">against UVB-induced photoaging in human dermal fibroblasts and hairless mice</cite>. While the snippet here is brief, the study supports a protective anti-photoaging effect in both cell and animal models.
- **Bifidobacterium breve B-3 (oral)**: chronic UV-irradiation experiments indicate that <cite id="7a3e7438-3">*B. breve* B-3 could potentially be used to prevent photoaging induced by chronic UV irradiation</cite>.

So, across models, various probiotics help by:
1. lowering **UVB/ROS-related oxidative stress** <cite id="00f1ed72-0,a1cf0ce7-0">and thereby reducing oxidative damage</cite>;
2. suppressing **inflammatory pathways** such as <cite id="d82f16ce-0">NF-κB</cite>;
3. limiting **matrix degradation** via reduced <cite id="d82f16ce-0">MMP-1 and MMP-3</cite> and related signaling (<cite id="d82f16ce-0">ERK and c-FOS</cite>);
4. improving skin outcomes like <cite id="00f1ed72-0">barrier function</cite>, and <cite id="d82f16ce-0,c1dcc3cc-0">reduced wrinkles, reduced epidermal/skin thickness, and less inflammation</cite>.

In short: probiotics in UVB-photoaging models work by dampening ROS-driven oxidative stress and downstream inflammatory/ECM-destructive signaling, which helps preserve collagen, barrier function, and overall skin appearance.

questions.original_query: What factors make the use of Botox and dermal fillers highly operator-dependent, and why do they share similar side effect profiles?

query.text: What factors make the use of Botox and dermal fillers highly operator-dependent, and why do they share similar side effect profiles?
query.answer: <cite id="26202001-1">Botox and dermal fillers are both very operator-dependent</cite> because good outcomes and safety rely heavily on <cite id="cb9f2f7c-0">injection techniques and knowledge of facial anatomy</cite>, while for botulinum toxin specifically <cite id="251719f5-5">muscle palpation and anatomical landmarks are insufficient to ensure the accuracy of BoNT-A injections</cite> and errors such as <cite id="251719f5-2">toxin placed close to the orbital rim or in excessive dose may diffuse toward extraocular muscles</cite>. They have <cite id="26202001-1">very similar side effects</cite> largely because many adverse events are common to facial injections themselves: for Botox, <cite id="1d1e105d-0">pain, edema, erythema, ecchymosis, and short-term hypesthesia</cite> can occur at any injection site, and for fillers, <cite id="1d1e105d-4">the most common adverse effects are local injection-related effects manifesting as erythema, edema, pain, and ecchymosis</cite>.
