query.text: What do cohort studies collectively reveal about the relationship between maternal vitamin D levels during pregnancy and the risk of wheeze in offspring?
query.answer: Five systematic reviews that pooled data from 4 to 6 cohort studies showed an association between vitamin D intake during pregnancy and wheeze among children. Overall, cohort evidence therefore points to a protective effect of higher maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy on offspring wheeze, with systematic reviews of observational studies indicating that mothers who had supplementation during pregnancy could decrease the risk of recurrent wheeze or asthma in their offspring. questions.original_query: What are the advantages of using carbon dioxide instead of air for insufflation during colonoscopy, and what are the clinical implications of its use?

query.text: What are the advantages of using carbon dioxide instead of air for insufflation during colonoscopy, and what are the clinical implications of its use?
query.answer:
Using carbon dioxide for insufflation during colonoscopy has several practical advantages over room air:

- <cite id="50332337-2">CO2 is absorbed up to 160 times faster</cite>, which helps explain why <cite id="50332337-7">insufflation of CO2 instead of air during colonoscopy can reduce distention-induced pain.</cite>
- Evidence from meta-analyses shows that <cite id="50332337-4">CO2 insufflation significantly reduces abdominal pain during and following the procedure lasting up to 24 hours.</cite>
- Compared with air, <cite id="50332337-6">CO2 insufflation during colonoscopy causes lower postprocedural pain and bowel distension without significant pCO2.</cite>
- Air insufflation is associated with symptoms that CO2 helps lessen, because <cite id="50332337-1">conventional air insufflation may cause prolonged abdominal bloating, excessive abdominal pain and discomfort during colonoscopy.</cite>

Clinical implications:
- Patients are likely to have <cite id="50332337-6">lower postprocedural pain and bowel distension</cite>, which can improve comfort and recovery after colonoscopy.
- Available evidence suggests this benefit does not come at a major respiratory safety cost in typical use, since studies found <cite id="50332337-6">no significant pCO2</cite> increase.
- The same general pattern has also been observed in pediatric populations: <cite id="50332337-3">CO2 insufflation reduces postprocedure pain and discomfort during pediatric colonoscopy</cite> and <cite id="50332337-8">may be reduced with the use of CO2 insufflation in pediatric GI endoscopies without a significant risk</cite>.

In short: CO2 insufflation mainly improves patient comfort by reducing bloating, distension, and pain during and after colonoscopy, while appearing clinically safe in routine practice.

questions.original_query: How do live birth and ongoing pregnancy rates compare between assisted reproductive technology cycles with and without endometrial compaction, considering various study conditions and protocols?

query.text: How do live birth and ongoing pregnancy rates compare between assisted reproductive technology cycles with and without endometrial compaction, considering various study conditions and protocols?
query.answer:
Overall, the best current synthesis suggests that <cite id="e3e184cc-0">live birth rates are essentially the same in ART cycles with and without endometrial compaction (EC), with pooled live birth RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.92–1.02) across 10 studies and 11,710 transfer cycles.</cite> The same meta-analysis also found that <cite id="e3e184cc-0">in euploid embryo-transfer subgroups, live birth remained similar with versus without EC (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.86–1.13; 4 studies, 1,172 cycles)</cite> and that <cite id="e3e184cc-0">miscarriage rates did not appear to differ by EC status (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.90–1.24).</cite>

For ongoing pregnancy, the picture is mixed across individual studies, but the overall direction is again toward <cite id="b8928e5b-9">similar live birth/ongoing pregnancy rates in cycles with or without EC.</cite> Some earlier studies reported benefit in selected settings—for example, <cite id="b8423c55-3">frozen euploid embryo transfer was reported to show improved ongoing pregnancy rates with endometrial compaction</cite>—but other studies did not confirm this. In particular, <cite id="b8928e5b-3">ongoing pregnancy rates did not differ among cycles with compaction</cite> in another report, and a large hormonal-replacement FET cohort found the opposite of a benefit: <cite id="691621c0-0">in over 16,000 hormonal replacement frozen-thawed embryo transfers, endometrial compaction was not associated with better pregnancy outcomes</cite>; after adjustment in Day-3 FETs, <cite id="691621c0-0">women with compacted endometrium had the lowest ongoing pregnancy rates and live birth rates among the comparison groups.</cite>

So, in concise terms: <cite id="e3e184cc-0">across ART cycles overall, EC does not reliably improve live birth</cite>, and <cite id="b8928e5b-9,e3e184cc-0">ongoing pregnancy rates are generally similar with and without EC when evidence is pooled.</cite> Apparent advantages in some subgroups—especially certain frozen/euploid or protocol-specific studies—<cite id="b8423c55-3">have not been consistent across studies</cite>, while large HRT-FET data even suggest <cite id="691621c0-0">no benefit, and possibly worse outcomes, with compaction in some protocols.</cite>

questions.original_query: How do elevated Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) levels and their regulation by gonadotropins and androgens contribute to follicular arrest in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?

query.text: How do elevated Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) levels and their regulation by gonadotropins and androgens contribute to follicular arrest in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?
query.answer:
<cite id="4e253367-3">PCOS patients have shown consistently higher levels of serum AMH</cite>, and this reflects <cite id="0d393fe4-0">both an increased number of small antral follicles and intrinsic overexpression of AMH by granulosa cells</cite>. In PCOS, that excess AMH is not just a marker; <cite id="4e253367-5">this excess of AMH is strongly suspected of playing a central role in the characteristic follicular arrest of PCOS</cite>.

Mechanistically, elevated AMH promotes follicular arrest because <cite id="0d393fe4-0">it suppresses FSH receptor (FSHR) expression in granulosa cells</cite>, <cite id="0d393fe4-0">directly inhibits CYP19A1 (aromatase)</cite>, and thereby <cite id="0d393fe4-0">reduces estradiol production</cite>. As a result, <cite id="0d393fe4-0">follicles accumulate in the small antral stage but fail to progress to ovulation</cite> and <cite id="0d393fe4-0">the low intrafollicular estradiol fails to support selection of a dominant follicle</cite>.

Its regulation by gonadotropins and androgens helps sustain this block. In PCOS, <cite id="0d393fe4-0">elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) relative to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)</cite> is a defining endocrine feature. <cite id="0d393fe4-0">LH acts on theca cells to stimulate androgen production, while these androgens act on granulosa cells to increase AMH expression</cite>; additionally, <cite id="0d393fe4-0">high LH may also directly increase AMH by upregulating AMH gene transcription in granulosa cells</cite>. Meanwhile, <cite id="0d393fe4-0">FSH normally suppresses AMH expression during follicular maturation</cite>, but in PCOS <cite id="0d393fe4-0">FSH levels are relatively low or granulosa cells are resistant to its action</cite>, so this normal brake on AMH is weakened. Hyperandrogenism strengthens the pattern further, since <cite id="4e253367-6">in PCOS with high androgen, serum AMH levels increase significantly compared with PCOS with normal androgen</cite>.

These interactions create a self-reinforcing loop: <cite id="0d393fe4-0">high LH and hyperandrogenism stimulate AMH expression, while low FSH and estradiol further exacerbate this dysregulation</cite>. On top of that, <cite id="4e253367-1">elevated AMH levels contribute to this dysregulation by increasing GnRH pulsatility, which leads to enhanced LH secretion</cite>. So the overall picture is that elevated AMH decreases follicular sensitivity to FSH and estrogen production, while LH-driven androgen excess keeps AMH high; together, <cite id="0d393fe4-0">these feedback loops contribute to follicular arrest and chronic anovulation</cite>.

without_scope.text: How do elevated Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) levels and their regulation by gonadotropins and androgens contribute to follicular arrest?
without_scope.answer:
Elevated AMH contributes to follicular arrest mainly by keeping growing follicles in an FSH-resistant, non-selected state. In PCOS, <cite id="4a02516e-0">serum AMH levels are 2–3 fold increased</cite> and this reflects <cite id="4a02516e-0">both increased number of small follicles and increased production per follicle.</cite> Normally, <cite id="4a02516e-0">AMH expression is the highest in preantral and small antral follicles up to 4 mm in diameter and declines in follicles selected for dominance.</cite> But in PCOS, <cite id="4a02516e-0">expression of AMH remains elevated in small antral follicles and its inhibition by FSH is absent, contributing to follicular arrest.</cite>

Mechanistically, high AMH suppresses the follicle’s ability to respond to FSH: <cite id="4a02516e-0">AMH can inhibit follicular growth in vitro and in vivo and decreases FSH sensitivity and follicle growth by reducing FSH receptor expression and aromatase expression.</cite> Reduced aromatase means less conversion of androgens to estrogens, which impairs dominant follicle selection. AMH may also block selection more directly because <cite id="4a02516e-0">increased AMH levels may contribute to follicular arrest by inhibiting follicle selection through suppression of the decrease in oocyte-derived growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9)</cite>; accordingly, <cite id="4a02516e-0">follicles from women with PCOS are blocked at the mid-antral stage.</cite>

Its regulation by gonadotropins and androgens helps reinforce this arrest. <cite id="4a02516e-0">The striking increase in AMH expression in women with PCOS is due to intrinsic dysregulation and various extrinsic influences including androgens and gonadotropins.</cite> Specifically, <cite id="4a02516e-0">AMH expression is regulated by androgens via the androgen receptor-β (AR)</cite> and <cite id="4a02516e-0">thecal androgen excess and AR signaling in granulosa cells are likely to contribute to the increased AMH expression in women with PCOS.</cite> On the gonadotropin side, <cite id="4a02516e-0">LH stimulates androgen production by theca cells and has been proposed to have a direct role in AMH regulation in granulosa cells.</cite> Meanwhile, although <cite id="4a02516e-0">the inhibitory effect of FSH on AMH expression, observed in women without PCOS</cite> would normally help follicles progress, <cite id="4a02516e-0">it appears to be absent in anovulatory women with PCOS.</cite>

So the overall picture is a self-reinforcing loop: excess LH promotes androgen production; androgens upregulate AMH; high AMH lowers FSH responsiveness and aromatase, preventing estrogenic maturation and dominant follicle selection; and loss of normal FSH-mediated AMH suppression lets this state persist, producing follicular arrest. <cite id="18262799-3">Abnormal secretion of FSH and LH leads to follicular arrest</cite> and <cite id="18262799-3">high AMH inhibits aromatase (CYP19A1)</cite>, reinforcing the same mechanism.

without_term.answer: In <cite id="7827df63-1">PCOS, a common type of hormone imbalance in women</cite>, <cite id="c7a0dcfe-2">anovulation is characterized by arrest of antral follicle development before the mature, preovulatory stage</cite>. A major driver is <cite id="7827df63-3">elevated levels of androgens, which may negatively impact follicular development, causing atresia</cite>. At the same time, <cite id="c7a0dcfe-3">elevated serum AMH inhibits the FSH-dependent factors necessary for follicle dominance</cite> and <cite id="9fb91019-7">AMH has an inhibitory action on FSH-induced aromatase</cite>, so follicles fail to complete maturation. In addition, <cite id="9fb91019-3">LH is believed to be behind the elevated production of AMH from granulosa cells of polycystic ovaries</cite>. Together, these hormone excesses and cross-regulatory loops trap follicles in a persistent immature state, producing the follicular arrest typical of PCOS.

questions.original_query: Which microRNAs have been consistently found to be differentially expressed in granulosa and cumulus cells of women with PCOS, and what potential roles do they play?

query.text: Which microRNAs have been consistently found to be differentially expressed in granulosa and cumulus cells of women with PCOS, and what potential roles do they play?
query.answer:
The most consistently recurrent miRNAs reported as altered in <cite id="00a59ce9-3">PCOS cumulus cells</cite> and/or <cite id="1bdaecac-0">granulosa cells</cite> are <cite id="1bdaecac-2,2acdccd1-3">miR-93 and miR-21</cite> and <cite id="1bdaecac-2,2acdccd1-2">miR-320/miR-320a and miR-132</cite>. In granulosa cells, <cite id="00a59ce9-2">miR-93 and miR-21 showed significantly increased levels</cite>, and review-level summaries note that <cite id="2acdccd1-3,3cadb4c4-0">free testosterone/free androgen index positively correlate with miR-21 and miR-93 in PCOS granulosa cells</cite>, suggesting roles as <cite id="2acdccd1-5">androgen-dependent factors</cite>. Functionally, <cite id="1bdaecac-1">miR-93-5p was elevated in PCOS and involved in proliferation, apoptosis and ferroptosis by regulating NF-κB/TXNIP signaling</cite>.  

In cumulus/cumulus-granulosa cells, <cite id="2acdccd1-2">miR-132 and miR-320 were expressed at low levels in women with PCOS</cite> and are <cite id="fba9072e-3">closely associated with estradiol secretion</cite>. More specifically, <cite id="3cadb4c4-5">miR-320a expression is significantly down-regulated in primary cumulus cells from PCOS patients</cite>, and this <cite id="3cadb4c4-5,3cadb4c4-2">down-regulation promotes estrogen deficiency / impairs steroidogenesis through RUNX2</cite>. A related recurrent cumulus-cell miRNA is <cite id="fba9072e-5,1bdaecac-5">miR-509-3p, whose reduced expression in PCOS cumulus cells is linked to estrogen deficiency</cite>; mechanistically, <cite id="fba9072e-5">miRNA-509-3p promotes oestradiol secretion by targeting MAP3K8</cite>.  

So, in short, the clearest repeatedly implicated miRNAs are <cite id="1bdaecac-2,2acdccd1-3">miR-93 and miR-21</cite> in granulosa cells and <cite id="2acdccd1-2,3cadb4c4-5">miR-132 and miR-320/320a</cite> in cumulus/cumulus-granulosa cells, with <cite id="fba9072e-5">miR-509-3p</cite> also emerging as an important cumulus-cell regulator. Their proposed roles center on <cite id="1bdaecac-1">granulosa-cell proliferation/apoptosis/ferroptosis</cite>, <cite id="2acdccd1-5,3cadb4c4-0">androgen responsiveness</cite>, and <cite id="fba9072e-3,3cadb4c4-2,fba9072e-5">steroidogenesis and estradiol production</cite>.

without_scope.text: Which microRNAs have been consistently found to be differentially expressed in granulosa and cumulus cells, and what potential roles do they play?
without_scope.answer:
The clearest comparative human study found <cite id="53b97d38-0">53 miRNAs differentially expressed between cumulus cells (CCs) and mural granulosa cells (MGCs)</cite>, with several miRNAs highlighted as functionally important in a consistent cell-type pattern.

**Higher in cumulus cells (CCs):**
- <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-146a-5p, miR-149-5p, and miR-509-3p were highly expressed in CCs and were linked to extracellular matrix remodeling</cite>.  
  - In particular, <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-146a-5p and miR-149-5p were positively correlated with PTX3 expression</cite>, and <cite id="53b97d38-0">PTX3 is an important extracellular matrix component required for cumulus-oocyte complex expansion</cite>.
- <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-182-5p was overexpressed in cumulus cells and strongly correlated with PTGS2 expression</cite>, suggesting a role in <cite id="53b97d38-0">oocyte maturation and cumulus expansion</cite>.
- <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-224-5p was highly expressed in CCs</cite> and may support <cite id="53b97d38-0">cell-to-cell interaction with the oocyte</cite>; the paper further notes that <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-224 can facilitate TGF-β-mediated proliferation and granulosa/cumulus expansion by targeting SMAD4</cite>.
- <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-378a-3p was elevated in cumulus cells</cite> and is implicated in <cite id="53b97d38-0">steroidogenesis</cite>; specifically, <cite id="53b97d38-0">it has been proposed as a negative regulator of aromatase transcript and estradiol production and also regulates cumulus-oocyte complex expansion</cite>.

**Higher in mural granulosa cells (MGCs):**
- <cite id="53b97d38-0">miR-1-3p, miR-34a-5p, miR-136-3p, miR-182-5p, miR-223-3p, and miR-410-3p were highly expressed in MGCs</cite>, and these were associated with <cite id="53b97d38-0">luteinization</cite>, supporting the distinct post-ovulatory role of mural granulosa cells.

**Overall interpretation:**
These findings suggest that the miRNAs most consistently highlighted in CCs vs granulosa/mural granulosa cells are:
- **CC-associated:** miR-146a-5p, miR-149-5p, miR-509-3p, miR-182-5p, miR-224-5p, miR-378a-3p  
- **MGC-associated:** miR-1-3p, miR-34a-5p, miR-136-3p, miR-223-3p, miR-410-3p  

Functionally, they appear to regulate <cite id="53b97d38-0">extracellular matrix remodeling, cumulus expansion, oocyte-cumulus communication, steroidogenesis, cell survival, ovulation, and luteinization</cite>.

questions.original_query: What evidence supports the anti-inflammatory and cartilage-protective effects of chondroitin sulfate and glucosamine sulfate in the treatment of osteoarthritis?

query.text: What evidence supports the anti-inflammatory and cartilage-protective effects of chondroitin sulfate and glucosamine sulfate in the treatment of osteoarthritis?
query.answer: Evidence for anti-inflammatory and cartilage-protective effects is suggestive, but stronger for some formulations and outcomes than others. - For chondroitin sulfate (CS), reviews report that it has been used in OA not only for symptom relief but also for possible disease modification, including “limiting cartilage volume loss and joint space narrowing progression.” Mechanistically, anti-inflammatory activity has been described: CS “prevents joint space narrowing and reduces joint swelling and effusion” and “elicits an anti-inflammatory” effect. Structural benefit is also supported by clinical summary evidence, where daily CS use was associated with reduced progression of medial knee joint-space narrowing and by updated meta-analytic work on “structure-modifying effects of chondroitin sulfate in knee osteoarthritis”. - For glucosamine sulfate (GS), mechanistic and preclinical data indicate biologic plausibility: in vitro and in vivo studies have shown effects on cartilage, synovium, and subchondral bone, with “structure-modifying and anti-inflammatory effects”. However, the same review emphasizes that clinical evidence for structure modification is “sparse” and that measured benefit depends strongly on formulation and trial quality. Still, one major synthesis found “highly significant efficacy of glucosamine on all outcomes, including joint space narrowing and WOMAC.” - For the combination of glucosamine and chondroitin, some laboratory evidence suggests cartilage-protective actions; for example, glucosamine hydrochloride combined with chondroitin sulfate in bovine cartilage explants inhibited degradative processes. But this does not by itself prove clinical cartilage protection in humans. Overall, the best-supported conclusion is that pharmacologic-grade chondroitin sulfate may have clinically meaningful benefits, including possible chondroprotection, while glucosamine sulfate has plausible anti-inflammatory/structure-modifying mechanisms but weaker and more inconsistent human structural evidence. Also, not all authorities agree: some guidance states there is no proof these agents slow degeneration or restore cartilage. So the evidence is mixed, with the most convincing support centered on selected high-quality CS preparations and some GS trials/meta-analyses.

without_scope.text: What evidence supports the anti-inflammatory and cartilage-protective effects of chondroitin sulfate and glucosamine sulfate?
without_scope.answer:
Evidence comes from both <cite id="340180b3-0">mechanistic studies showing glucosamine sulfate inhibits IL‑1β–driven proinflammatory mediator synthesis through an NF‑κB–dependent mechanism in human osteoarthritic chondrocytes</cite> and from reviews concluding that <cite id="340180b3-3">glucosamine exerts chondroprotective effects and effectively reduces OA pain and stiffness</cite>. A broader review of cartilage biology also reports that <cite id="340180b3-5">inhibition of the IL‑1β–induced NF‑κB pathway by glucosamine sulfate results in reduced synthesis of the COX‑2 enzyme</cite>, supporting an anti-inflammatory mode of action.

For chondroitin sulfate, reviews describe both anti-inflammatory and structure-protective effects: <cite id="8c4ce233-1">chondroitin sulfate prevents joint space narrowing and reduces joint swelling and effusion, and to produce these effects it elicits an anti-inflammatory action</cite>. Clinical structural evidence is also reported, with <cite id="8c4ce233-5">chondroitin sulfate treatment significantly reducing cartilage volume loss in knee osteoarthritis starting at 6 months, and bone marrow lesions at 12 months</cite>. A recent critical review likewise summarizes that <cite id="c41b5e04-0">chondroitin sulfate has been used for disease-modifying properties by limiting cartilage volume loss and joint space narrowing progression</cite>, though it also notes <cite id="c41b5e04-0">inconsistencies in published trials and the need for high-quality standardized pharmacologic-grade preparations</cite>.

So, the best-supported picture is:
- **Glucosamine sulfate:** anti-inflammatory signaling evidence, especially via <cite id="340180b3-0,340180b3-5">IL‑1β/NF‑κB inhibition and reduced COX‑2/proinflammatory mediator production</cite>.
- **Chondroitin sulfate:** anti-inflammatory activity plus some **cartilage-protective structural evidence**, including <cite id="8c4ce233-1,8c4ce233-5">less joint space narrowing, less swelling/effusion, and reduced cartilage volume loss</cite>.
- **Caveat:** overall clinical efficacy remains <cite id="c41b5e04-0">mixed across trials, partly due to differences in product quality and study design</cite>.

questions.original_query: What risk factors should clinicians consider before starting JAK inhibitors in patients with refractory rheumatoid arthritis?

query.text: What risk factors should clinicians consider before starting JAK inhibitors in patients with refractory rheumatoid arthritis?
query.answer:
Before starting a JAK inhibitor in refractory RA, clinicians should especially assess whether the patient is in a <cite id="d29ede65-1,ee08f836-6">higher-risk group defined by age ≥65, current or past long-term smoking, or other baseline cardiovascular or malignancy risk factors</cite>. They should also consider <cite id="ee08f836-1,ee08f836-8,d29ede65-6">prior venous thromboembolism or other VTE risk factors</cite>, because regulators warn that these drugs are associated with <cite id="0d4ed013-0,0d4ed013-7">increased risks of serious heart-related events, cancer, blood clots, and death</cite>. Risk appears to be influenced by the patient’s starting risk profile, with <cite id="ee08f836-0,d29ede65-0,90d170a4-0">baseline cardiovascular risk modifying the likelihood of cardiovascular and cancer harms</cite>.

In addition, clinicians should screen carefully for infection risk before initiation: <cite id="23f4e804-1,0c9dc71b-1">patients should be screened for tuberculosis before treatment, and active TB is a reason not to start therapy</cite>; <cite id="23f4e804-5,0c9dc71b-5">hepatitis B/C screening is recommended, and initiation is not recommended in active hepatitis B or C</cite>. Baseline labs also matter, because <cite id="0c9dc71b-2,0c9dc71b-4">JAK inhibitors should not be started when lymphocyte, neutrophil, or hemoglobin values are too low, or when liver tests are significantly abnormal</cite>.

query.answer: <cite id="78e58d8e-4">MRI should not be used routinely for the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS).</cite> It is particularly useful when clinicians need to <cite id="d27843cf-2">exclude secondary causes of CTS</cite>, especially to <cite id="6ce72acf-6">search for an occult mass or space-occupying lesion</cite>. This is especially relevant in <cite id="a8f1bdd8-0">unilateral CTS</cite>, where <cite id="a8f1bdd8-3">special tests such as CT or MRI are important to identify a space-occupying lesion</cite>. questions.original_query: What are the main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty compared to total knee arthroplasty with respect to anatomical preservation and postoperative recovery?

query.text: What are the main benefits of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty compared to total knee arthroplasty with respect to anatomical preservation and postoperative recovery?
query.answer:
Compared with total knee arthroplasty, unicompartmental knee arthroplasty mainly benefits patients by <cite id="3b8bfe95-3,504fd8d3-1,504fd8d3-6">preserving more of the native knee anatomy—including healthy bone and cartilage, with better preservation of bone stock and more natural knee kinematics/“natural-feeling” joint function</cite>. It is also <cite id="f200f82b-1,3b8bfe95-2">less invasive, with more limited exposure and less soft-tissue disruption</cite>. 

For postoperative recovery, UKA is associated with <cite id="3b8bfe95-0,3b8bfe95-3,504fd8d3-2">faster rehabilitation and shorter recovery</cite>, as well as <cite id="3b8bfe95-1,3b8bfe95-5,f200f82b-2">less postoperative pain</cite>. Studies and clinical sources also report <cite id="f200f82b-0,504fd8d3-2,3b8bfe95-3">better early range of motion, shorter hospital stay, and less blood loss</cite>. Overall, the main advantages are <cite id="3b8bfe95-3,504fd8d3-1">greater anatomical preservation and a quicker, less painful early recovery than TKA</cite>.

questions.original_query: What effects do aerobic exercise interventions have on inflammatory markers and disease activity in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?

query.text: What effects do aerobic exercise interventions have on inflammatory markers and disease activity in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?
query.answer:
In rheumatoid arthritis, aerobic exercise interventions appear to have <cite id="de218a0a-0">beneficial and safe</cite> effects overall, but their impact is stronger on symptoms and function than on most inflammatory biomarkers.

- On disease activity: broader exercise evidence shows <cite id="88329916-0">significant reductions in disease activity score in joints (DAS)</cite> and also improvement in symptoms such as <cite id="88329916-0">fatigue</cite> and <cite id="88329916-0">pain intensity</cite>.
- On inflammatory markers: the same umbrella meta-analysis found a <cite id="88329916-0">significant reduction in ESR</cite>, but <cite id="88329916-0">no significant impact on other inflammatory biomarkers was observed</cite>.
- For aerobic exercise specifically: a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs in RA found that aerobic exercise <cite id="de218a0a-0">can improve functional ability</cite>, <cite id="de218a0a-0">relieve pain</cite>, and <cite id="de218a0a-0">increase aerobic capacity</cite>, concluding that it <cite id="de218a0a-0">has a certain alleviating effect on the disease</cite>.

So, the best concise summary is: <cite id="88329916-0,de218a0a-0">aerobic exercise in RA generally improves disease-related outcomes such as pain, function, aerobic fitness, and likely lowers disease activity, while effects on inflammation are modest and inconsistent—ESR may decrease, but most other biomarkers do not show clear, consistent improvement.</cite>

questions.original_query: What are the additional benefits of preoperative manometry beyond its role in determining the surgical approach for gastroesophageal reflux disease?

query.text: What are the additional benefits of preoperative manometry beyond its role in determining the surgical approach for gastroesophageal reflux disease?
query.answer:
Beyond helping choose the operative technique, preoperative manometry is useful because it can:

- <cite id="773ef94e-0">rule out major esophageal motility disorders</cite>, which helps avoid inappropriate antireflux surgery in patients whose symptoms may be due to another motor disorder rather than GERD.
- <cite id="773ef94e-0">help confirm that the preoperative evaluation is identifying appropriate surgical candidates</cite>.
- <cite id="e0d83731-2">be used before an esophageal pH (impedance) test</cite>, so it has value in facilitating reflux testing as part of the diagnostic workup.
- <cite id="773ef94e-0">assess peristaltic reserve prior to surgery</cite>; additionally, <cite id="e0d83731-1">multiple rapid swallows during manometry may help predict postoperative dysphagia</cite>.
- <cite id="773ef94e-0">help assess the presence of an underlying hiatal hernia</cite> when provocative maneuvers are added to HRM.

So, in short: manometry adds diagnostic, screening, and prognostic value—not just guidance on which surgery to perform.

without_term.text: What are the additional benefits of preoperative pressure testing beyond its role in determining the surgical approach for acid reflux disease?
without_term.answer:
Beyond helping choose the operation itself, preoperative pressure testing (esophageal manometry/HRM) offers several other benefits:

- It <cite id="a53de1a3-0">helps confirm the diagnosis of GERD</cite>.
- It <cite id="a53de1a3-0">rules out major esophageal motility disorders</cite> and can <cite id="f46540a9-1">identify disorders that could contraindicate surgery</cite>.
- It <cite id="a53de1a3-0">helps select appropriate surgical candidates</cite>.
- With provocative maneuvers, it can <cite id="a53de1a3-0">assess for underlying hiatal hernias</cite> and <cite id="a53de1a3-0">test the patient’s peristaltic reserve prior to surgery</cite>, which is useful for anticipating postoperative swallowing function.
- It can also support reflux testing, since manometry is used to <cite id="2f87ffb5-5">localize the lower esophageal sphincter for accurate placement of the pH electrode</cite>.

So, its added value is diagnostic and risk-stratifying: it confirms true reflux disease, excludes mimicking/contraindicating motility problems, identifies better surgical candidates, and improves related pH testing.

query.text: How do remission rates for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) vary five years after different bariatric surgeries in patients with a BMI of 25 or higher?
query.answer:
<cite id="77ec749b-0">Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch as well as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass have demonstrated higher rates of T2DM resolution when compared with other bariatric procedures.</cite> 

A concise 5-year ranking is:

- <cite id="77ec749b-0">Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD/DS)</cite>: highest remission
- <cite id="77ec749b-0">Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB)</cite>: next highest
- Sleeve gastrectomy (SG): lower than RYGB
- Adjustable gastric banding (AGB): lowest among the common procedures

For a direct 5-year head-to-head example, <cite id="7cf9f313-1">diabetes remission 5 years postprocedure was significantly higher after SR-LRYGB (47 vs. 33%, P < 0.01)</cite>, meaning bypass outperformed sleeve gastrectomy in that trial.  

So, in patients with <cite id="77ec749b-0">BMI ≥ 25 kg/m²</cite> undergoing metabolic/bariatric surgery, remission at about five years generally appears greatest after BPD/DS, followed by RYGB, then SG, with AGB producing the lowest long-term remission.

without_scope.text: How do remission rates for type 2 diabetes mellitus vary after different bariatric surgeries?
without_scope.answer:
Remission rates for type 2 diabetes after bariatric surgery <cite id="c54d023e-0">vary widely, roughly from 45% to 95% depending on the procedure</cite>. In general, <cite id="c54d023e-0">procedures that induce greater weight loss are associated with higher rates of diabetes remission</cite>.

A practical ranking is:

- **Biliopancreatic diversion/duodenal switch (BPD/DS): highest remission**
  - <cite id="08d0e2d5-0">BPD/DS patients had about a 229% increase in odds of remission at 1 year versus RYGB (adjusted OR 3.29)</cite>, suggesting the strongest remission effect among common operations.

- **Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB): high remission**
  - In one meta-analysis, <cite id="70ba436f-5">the overall remission rate was 83.75% with RYGB</cite>.
  - In longer-term real-world follow-up, <cite id="08d0e2d5-8">remission was 24.5% after RYGB</cite>, showing that rates decline over time and depend on how remission is defined.

- **Sleeve gastrectomy (SG): moderate-to-high remission, usually somewhat lower than RYGB**
  - <cite id="70ba436f-5">the same meta-analysis reported 71.6% remission with SG</cite>.
  - Longer-term observational data found <cite id="08d0e2d5-8">15.2% remission after SG</cite>.
  - A head-to-head trial also found <cite id="08d0e2d5-2">47% remission after banded RYGB versus 33% after sleeve gastrectomy</cite> at 5 years.

- **Adjustable gastric banding (AGB): lowest remission among these common procedures**
  - <cite id="70ba436f-5">meta-analytic remission was 47.9% with AGB</cite>.
  - In longer-term practice data, <cite id="08d0e2d5-8">remission was 8.9% with adjustable gastric banding</cite>.

Overall: <cite id="70ba436f-5">RYGB tends to produce higher remission than sleeve gastrectomy, and both generally outperform adjustable gastric banding</cite>; <cite id="08d0e2d5-0">BPD/DS appears to produce the highest remission rates of all</cite>. The exact percentages differ substantially by <cite id="c54d023e-0">procedure</cite>, follow-up duration, and remission definition.

questions.original_query: How do incomplete blinking and lagophthalmos resulting from orbicularis oculi paralysis influence tear film stability and contribute to dry eye symptoms?

query.text: How do incomplete blinking and lagophthalmos resulting from orbicularis oculi paralysis influence tear film stability and contribute to dry eye symptoms?
query.answer:
<cite id="ff09191f-0">A full eyelid closure with a normal blink reflex is necessary for the maintenance of a stable tear film and healthy ocular surface.</cite> When the <cite id="ff09191f-0">primary cause of lagophthalmos is facial nerve paralysis</cite>, the resulting orbicularis oculi weakness/paralysis prevents complete blinking and lid closure. 

This affects the tear film in two main ways:  
1. <cite id="8eedc760-0">Incomplete blinking contributes to tear film instability</cite>, and <cite id="8eedc760-3">can lead to inadequate tear distribution, promoting tear film instability</cite>.  
2. With poor closure, the eye is left exposed; patients <cite id="ff09191f-0">are at risk of corneal exposure, evaporation of the tear film, and subsequent exposure keratopathy.</cite>

Functionally, an incomplete blink also fails to refresh the ocular surface normally: <cite id="8eedc760-7">partial blinks are not sufficient to refresh the tear film</cite> and are not sufficient <cite id="8eedc760-7">to induce lipid secretion</cite>, which further weakens the tear film’s anti-evaporative protection.

So, incomplete blinking and lagophthalmos from orbicularis oculi paralysis destabilize the tear film by reducing tear spreading/refreshing and increasing ocular surface exposure and evaporation. The result is the typical dry-eye symptom pattern: <cite id="db18b0dd-1">dry and irritated eyes</cite>, with possible <cite id="db18b0dd-9">itching or scratchy eyes, foreign body sensation, tearing, [and] crusting</cite>.

questions.original_query: What clinical evidence and study designs support the effectiveness of Botulinum Toxin A (BoNT/A) in treating pain associated with diabetic neuropathy?

query.text: What clinical evidence and study designs support the effectiveness of Botulinum Toxin A (BoNT/A) in treating pain associated with diabetic neuropathy?
query.answer:
The clinical evidence for BoNT/A in painful diabetic neuropathy is based mainly on <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">randomized controlled trials comparing BTX-A with placebo in DPN pain</cite>, supplemented by meta-analyses/systematic reviews that pool those trials.

**Highest-level evidence**
- A 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis found <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">three randomized controlled trials with 100 patients were included</cite>.
- In the pooled analysis, <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">the BTX-A group had a reduced VAS score compared with the placebo group at 1 month (MD: -2.30), 2 months (MD: -2.66), and 3 months (MD: -2.21)</cite>.
- The same review also reported broader patient benefit: <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">BTX-A treatment also improved sleep and life quality</cite>, while <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">there was no difference in adverse effects between the two groups</cite>.
- The review’s overall interpretation was cautious but positive: <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">limited evidence demonstrated that BTX-A could significantly relieve pain and improve sleep and life quality for DPN pain patients</cite>.

**Earlier meta-analytic support**
- An earlier meta-analysis reported that <cite id="63abd33e-5">two studies on PDN were analyzed in the meta-analysis showing improvement of 1.96 VAS points (95% CI, -3.09 to -0.84; Z score = 3.43, P < 0.001)</cite>.

**Study designs used in the primary clinical trials**
- One key trial used a <cite id="63abd33e-9">double-blind crossover trial of intradermal BoNT/A for diabetic neuropathic pain in 18 patients</cite>.
- Another trial framework in this literature is described as <cite id="63abd33e-3">the effect of intradermal botulinum toxin A injections on painful DPN</cite> and aimed to <cite id="63abd33e-3">determine the effective intradermal dosage of BTX-A</cite>, indicating a dose-finding randomized clinical design.
- More broadly, the neuropathic pain BoNT literature includes <cite id="63abd33e-6">a randomized, prospective double blind, parallel design study</cite>, consistent with the placebo-controlled RCT approach summarized in the DPN meta-analysis.

**What this means**
- The evidence supporting effectiveness is strongest from <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">randomized controlled trials</cite> and pooled analyses of those trials.
- The designs include <cite id="63abd33e-9">double-blind crossover</cite> and <cite id="63abd33e-6">prospective double-blind parallel</cite> placebo-controlled studies, with treatment delivered <cite id="63abd33e-9">intradermally</cite>.
- Overall, current evidence suggests BoNT/A is effective for reducing painful diabetic neuropathy symptoms, but <cite id="ac39b0a8-0">more larger well-designed trials are required</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What evidence and study designs support the effectiveness of a treatment in treating pain associated with neuropathy?
fully_underspecified.answer:
The strongest support for a neuropathy-pain treatment usually comes from:

1. **Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials**  
   These are the key studies used to show whether the treatment reduces neuropathic pain better than placebo while limiting bias.

2. **Active-comparator randomized trials**  
   These compare the treatment against an established neuropathic-pain therapy to show similar or better effectiveness.

3. **Crossover trials**  
   Common in pain research, these let the same patient receive both treatment and control at different times, which can improve sensitivity for detecting pain relief.

4. **Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs**  
   These provide the highest-level summary of whether a treatment works across multiple studies and patient groups.

5. **Longer-term extension or pragmatic studies**  
   These help show whether benefits are durable and clinically meaningful in real-world use, beyond short-term trial settings.

In neuropathy studies, effectiveness is typically supported when trials show improvements in outcomes such as:
- average daily pain score,
- proportion of patients achieving at least 30% or 50% pain reduction,
- sleep interference,
- physical function, and
- quality of life.

without_scope.text: What clinical evidence and study designs support the effectiveness of Botulinum Toxin A (BoNT/A) in treating pain?
without_scope.answer:
## Overall picture

Clinical support for BoNT/A in pain is strongest for <cite id="9a2a491d-0">chronic migraine</cite> and is supported by <cite id="35dd2e7c-5">meta-analysis</cite>, while evidence also supports benefit in <cite id="59f41499-2">neuropathic pain</cite> and specifically <cite id="59f41499-0">trigeminal neuralgia (TN) and peripheral neuropathic pain (PNP)</cite>. At the same time, the evidence base is not uniformly positive across all pain syndromes: for <cite id="9946618d-0">chronic musculoskeletal pain, one systematic review did not support adjunctive BoNT-A use</cite>, and another broader review concluded that <cite id="9946618d-1">evidence was still insufficient to support routine use in chronic pain overall</cite>.

## Strongest evidence: chronic migraine

The best-established analgesic indication is chronic migraine. Two large PREEMPT trials provided pivotal evidence: <cite id="9a2a491d-1">PREEMPT 1 and 2 were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies with 1,384 patients across 122 sites</cite>. Their pooled analysis found that <cite id="9a2a491d-0">onabotulinumtoxinA is an effective prophylactic treatment for chronic migraine</cite>, and a Cochrane-based meta-analysis reported that <cite id="35dd2e7c-5">botulinum toxin reduced migraine frequency by about 2.0 migraine days per month versus placebo in chronic migraineurs</cite>. Review articles also summarize that <cite id="6abb9244-1">efficacy in chronic migraine was shown in two large industry-sponsored randomized controlled clinical trials</cite> and that <cite id="6abb9244-4">PREEMPT data showed a mean reduction of approximately 2 headache days over 4 weeks compared with placebo</cite>.

### Study designs used in chronic migraine
The core supporting designs were <cite id="9a2a491d-1">large multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials</cite>, followed by <cite id="35dd2e7c-5">systematic review/meta-analysis pooling trial data</cite>. This is the highest-quality clinical evidence represented in the retrieved sources.

## Neuropathic pain: supportive but less definitive evidence

For neuropathic pain, several reviews and meta-analyses report benefit, but usually with more caution than in migraine. A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis concluded that <cite id="59f41499-2">RCT evidence supports the role of Botulinum toxin A for neuropathic pain, but failed to provide evidence for its use as first-line treatment</cite>. Another review found that <cite id="35dd2e7c-2">BoNT-A is safe for treating neuropathic pain, without notable side effects, and its effect is durable</cite>. Earlier review literature similarly notes that <cite id="6abb9244-0">placebo-controlled studies support an antinociceptive effect of BoNT/A in neuropathic pain</cite>.

### Study designs used in neuropathic pain
The evidence here comes mainly from <cite id="59f41499-2">randomized controlled trials</cite>, often <cite id="6abb9244-0">placebo-controlled</cite>, synthesized in <cite id="35dd2e7c-2">systematic reviews and meta-analyses</cite>. Compared with migraine, these studies are generally smaller and more heterogeneous, which is why reviews stop short of recommending BoNT/A as <cite id="59f41499-2">first-line therapy</cite>.

## Trigeminal neuralgia and peripheral neuropathic pain

Within neuropathic pain, TN has especially consistent clinical support. A meta-analysis reported that <cite id="59f41499-0">BTX-A provides significant benefit in patients with TN and PNP compared with placebo</cite>, and another review concluded that <cite id="59f41499-7">the evidence suggests a clinically significant benefit in trigeminal neuralgia</cite>. Individual randomized trial evidence also exists: one study reported that <cite id="59f41499-5">40 patients completed the trial and BTX-A significantly reduced pain intensity by week 2 and attack frequency by week 1</cite>.

### Study designs used in TN/PNP
Support comes from both <cite id="59f41499-5">individual randomized trials</cite> and <cite id="59f41499-0,59f41499-7">systematic reviews/meta-analyses</cite>. Some ongoing work is still using <cite id="59f41499-6">double-blind randomized clinical trial</cite> designs, showing that the field continues to rely on controlled comparative methods to refine the evidence base.

## Musculoskeletal and myofascial pain: mixed evidence

Evidence is less consistent in chronic musculoskeletal pain. One systematic review concluded that <cite id="9946618d-0">the available data do not support BoNT-A as an adjunctive therapy for chronic musculoskeletal pain</cite>. However, another meta-analysis found that <cite id="9946618d-4">BoNTA had a small to moderate analgesic effect in chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions</cite>, and a review summarized that <cite id="9946618d-2">three RCTs showed BoNT-A improved pain, function, or both better than saline, acupuncture, or steroid injections</cite>. 

### Study designs used in musculoskeletal pain
This area includes <cite id="9946618d-2">RCTs with active comparators or saline control</cite> and <cite id="9946618d-0,9946618d-4">systematic reviews/meta-analyses</cite>. The conflicting conclusions suggest heterogeneity in patient populations, injection techniques, comparator treatments, and outcomes.

## What study designs support BoNT/A for pain?

Across the retrieved literature, the main designs are:

- <cite id="9a2a491d-1">Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trials</cite> — strongest example: chronic migraine PREEMPT studies.  
- <cite id="59f41499-5">Smaller randomized controlled trials</cite> — common in trigeminal neuralgia and other focal neuropathic pain syndromes.  
- <cite id="35dd2e7c-5,35dd2e7c-2,59f41499-0,9946618d-0">Systematic reviews and meta-analyses</cite> — used to pool evidence across trials and indications.  
- <cite id="9946618d-2">Trials versus active comparators such as acupuncture or steroid injections</cite> — especially in musculoskeletal pain.  

## Bottom line

The clinical evidence for BoNT/A analgesia is most convincing in <cite id="9a2a491d-0,35dd2e7c-5">chronic migraine</cite>, where large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials and meta-analyses show benefit. There is also meaningful evidence for <cite id="59f41499-2,59f41499-0">neuropathic pain, especially trigeminal neuralgia and peripheral neuropathic pain</cite>, but reviews indicate it is <cite id="59f41499-2">not yet supported as first-line treatment</cite>. For <cite id="9946618d-0,9946618d-4">musculoskeletal pain, evidence is mixed</cite>, so effectiveness appears more indication-specific than universal.

questions.original_query: What evidence supports a link between mycotoxin-induced intestinal changes and those seen in inflammatory bowel diseases?

query.text: What evidence supports a link between mycotoxin-induced intestinal changes and those seen in inflammatory bowel diseases?
query.answer: The main evidence is that <cite id="3438f616-0">mycotoxins downregulate mucin and tight junction proteins, increasing gut permeability as seen in IBD</cite>. This matters because <cite id="7f836a74-1">IBD patients demonstrate a loss of tight junction barrier function, increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and immune</cite> activation, while <cite id="796d184f-2">mycotoxins induce a pro-inflammatory cytokine response and disrupt the gut microbiota</cite>. The overlap extends to microbial and redox pathways: <cite id="3438f616-9">IBD is often accompanied by dysbiosis, and persistent dysbiosis reciprocally aggravates inflammation</cite>, and <cite id="dd7a476b-3">Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota is one of the important factors contributing to the development of IBD</cite>; similarly, mycotoxin literature reports <cite id="796d184f-2">disrupt the gut microbiota</cite>. Oxidative stress is another shared feature, since <cite id="3438f616-1">oxidative stress can affect the progression and development of IBD by regulating the homeostasis of the gut microbiota and immune response</cite>. Together, these shared changes—<cite id="3438f616-0">mucin/tight-junction loss and increased permeability</cite>, <cite id="796d184f-2,7f836a74-1">pro-inflammatory immune signaling</cite>, and <cite id="796d184f-2,3438f616-9,dd7a476b-3,3438f616-1">dysbiosis/oxidative-stress-related inflammation</cite>—support a mechanistic link between mycotoxin-induced intestinal injury and intestinal changes typical of IBD, although this is mainly mechanistic overlap rather than proof that mycotoxins directly cause human IBD.

questions.original_query: How does Zoledronic Acid (ZA) affect macrophage polarization, and what are the underlying mechanisms involved?

query.text: How does Zoledronic Acid (ZA) affect macrophage polarization, and what are the underlying mechanisms involved?
query.answer: <cite id="1a405b68-0,02fc07a3-2,750e8059-1">Zoledronic acid (ZA) generally skews macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype while suppressing or impairing M2 polarization.</cite> <cite id="1a405b68-0,92414763-0">One key mechanism is that ZA enhances LPS-induced M1 polarization through an NLRP3 inflammasome-dependent pathway, rather than promoting M2 polarization.</cite> <cite id="92414763-1">This is associated with increased IL-1β expression and reduced IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1ra),</cite> <cite id="1a405b68-0">which helps drive inflammatory cytokine production.</cite> <cite id="02fc07a3-0,02fc07a3-1">A second mechanism is TLR4 signaling: ZA elevates TLR-4 expression in macrophages, and in TLR-4 knockout mice ZA-induced M1 polarization is reduced,</cite> <cite id="02fc07a3-0,02fc07a3-2">supporting a TLR4-mediated shift toward M1 and away from M2.</cite> <cite id="02fc07a3-6,750e8059-1">ZA also appears to blunt M2-associated functions by reducing IL-10 and impairing tumor-induced M2 polarization, thereby lowering macrophage pro-invasive and pro-angiogenic activity.</cite> Overall, <cite id="1a405b68-0,02fc07a3-0,750e8059-1">ZA promotes inflammatory, M1-like macrophage programming through NLRP3/IL-1β and TLR4-linked pathways while inhibiting M2-associated reparative or tumor-supportive responses.</cite>

For example, <cite id="f91169df-1">β-glucan promotes M1 polarization through the NF-κB/autophagy pathway</cite>, whereas <cite id="f91169df-4">Smilaparin A reduces polarization toward the M1 phenotype</cite>. questions.original_query: How do synthetic cathinones interact with monoamine transporters, and how do these interactions influence their pharmacological effects?

query.text: How do synthetic cathinones interact with monoamine transporters, and how do these interactions influence their pharmacological effects?
query.answer:
Synthetic cathinones act mainly by targeting the three plasma-membrane monoamine transporters—<cite id="0ae299f9-0">dopamine (DAT), norepinephrine (NET), and 5-HT (SERT)</cite>. <cite id="0ae299f9-0">They are psychomotor stimulants that impair the normal function of these transporters</cite>, and they do so in two broad ways:

1. <cite id="0ae299f9-0">Ring-substituted cathinones like mephedrone are transporter substrates that evoke neurotransmitter release by reversing the normal direction of transporter flux</cite>. In other words, they behave as “releasers.”
2. <cite id="0ae299f9-0">Pyrrolidine-containing cathinones like MDPV are potent transporter inhibitors that block neurotransmitter uptake</cite>. These act as “blockers.”

Although the mechanism differs, the net result is similar: <cite id="0ae299f9-0">all synthetic cathinones increase extracellular monoamine concentrations in the brain, thereby enhancing cell-to-cell monoamine signaling</cite>. That rise in dopamine, norepinephrine, and/or serotonin underlies their stimulant and psychoactive effects.

Transporter selectivity strongly shapes the pharmacology. Evidence indicates that <cite id="0ab6129b-5">all of the cathinones were potent NE uptake inhibitors but differed in their DA vs. 5-HT transporter inhibition profiles and monoamine release effects</cite>, and <cite id="0ab6129b-3">most of the compounds were more potent inhibitors of NET uptake</cite>. This helps explain prominent sympathetic effects such as <cite id="0ab6129b-2">hypertension</cite>.

Differences in DAT versus SERT action are especially important for behavioral effects. <cite id="3c834324-0">Drugs with a high DAT/SERT ratio will have high abuse potential</cite>, and <cite id="3c834324-1">a high DAT/SERT ratio indicates a likelihood for a drug to have reinforcing and rewarding effects</cite>. So, cathinones that preferentially elevate dopamine tend to produce stronger stimulant, reinforcing, and addiction-related effects, whereas compounds with relatively greater serotonergic action tend to have lower abuse liability and more MDMA-like subjective effects. At the toxic end, excessive monoamine signaling is associated with adverse psychiatric and autonomic outcomes such as <cite id="0ab6129b-2">paranoia and hallucinations</cite> in addition to <cite id="0ab6129b-2">hypertension</cite>.

In short: synthetic cathinones either <cite id="0ae299f9-0">reverse transporter flux to release monoamines</cite> or <cite id="0ae299f9-0">block monoamine reuptake</cite>; both actions <cite id="0ae299f9-0">increase extracellular monoamines</cite>. Their relative activity at <cite id="0ae299f9-0">DAT, NET, and SERT</cite> determines whether their effects are more reinforcing/stimulant-like, more serotonergic/entactogenic-like, or more autonomically toxic.

fully_underspecified.text: How do studies evaluate the timing of exposure and relate different exposure periods to children's outcomes?
fully_underspecified.answer: Studies typically use <cite id="S9,S56">longitudinal exposure data to test whether children’s outcomes reflect a sensitive/critical period, cumulative exposure, or recency of exposure</cite>. In practice, they often <cite id="S55,S59">define biologically meaningful windows—such as trimesters, months or weeks of gestation, infancy, preschool age, and middle childhood—and relate each window to later cognitive, behavioral, growth, respiratory, or other outcomes</cite>. Because <cite id="S57,S34">exposures measured across nearby periods are usually highly correlated, making separate period-by-period regressions unstable</cite>, studies increasingly use <cite id="S24,S28,S36">distributed lag or weighted cumulative exposure models to estimate week-by-week or month-by-month associations and identify sensitive windows</cite>, as well as <cite id="S18,S50">structured life-course models that formally compare whether a specific period, the accumulation of exposure, or more recent exposure best explains the outcome</cite>. When the goal is to compare broad periods directly, <cite id="S33,S58">multiple-informants or repeated-measures models test whether prenatal and postnatal associations differ in strength</cite>; and when exposure starts at different ages, <cite id="S61,S62">some studies compare children “treated by age x” versus “treated by age x+1” to estimate how age at first exposure relates to later outcomes</cite>.

questions.original_query: What does clinical research indicate about the efficacy and safety of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as an adjunctive treatment targeting oxidative stress in severe malaria?

query.text: What does clinical research indicate about the efficacy and safety of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as an adjunctive treatment targeting oxidative stress in severe malaria?
query.answer:
Clinical research to date does <cite id="5b4065d1-0">not support N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as an effective adjunctive treatment for severe falciparum malaria</cite>, despite the biological rationale that <cite id="5b4065d1-0">severe falciparum malaria is accompanied by oxidative stress and reduced red blood cell deformability</cite> and that NAC <cite id="5b4065d1-0">has anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, and vasodilating properties</cite>.

The key evidence is a <cite id="5b4065d1-0">randomised double blind placebo-controlled trial of 108 adults with severe falciparum malaria</cite>. In that study, <cite id="5b4065d1-0">there was no significant difference in mortality between the two groups (NAC = 6/54 versus placebo = 8/54, p = 0.572), lactate clearance times (NAC = 30.0 hours, placebo = 26.0 hours, p = 0.374) or coma recovery times (NAC = 22.5 hours, placebo = 24.0 hours, p = 0.953)</cite>. The trial also found that <cite id="5b4065d1-0">NAC treatment had no effect on blood pressure, lactate or lactate/pyruvate ratio</cite>, and in a physiologic substudy, <cite id="5b4065d1-0">there was no effect of NAC treatment on tissue oxygen saturation, tissue pH, or microvascular blood flow</cite>.

Regarding safety, the evidence suggests NAC was <cite id="9787b7eb-9">safe and well tolerated</cite>, and the trial reported <cite id="5b4065d1-0">no significant difference in the incidence of allergic reactions between NAC and placebo (1.8% versus 5.6%, p = 0.617), nor any other side effect due to NAC</cite>. However, an important caution emerged: <cite id="5b4065d1-0">there was a significantly slower parasite clearance time in the NAC group (96 versus 80 hours, p = 0.018), but this was only in the artesunate subgroup</cite>, and the authors concluded that <cite id="5b4065d1-0">in artesunate-treated patients, the addition of NAC may interfere with parasite clearance and should be used with caution</cite>.

There was some earlier preliminary suggestion of benefit: <cite id="5b4065d1-0">in a pilot study [NAC] improved lactate clearance in severe malaria patients treated with quinine</cite>. But the larger definitive trial found no clinical benefit, and review-level evidence summarizes that <cite id="9787b7eb-9">a RCT in 108 adults with SM showed NAC to be safe and well tolerated, but to have no effect on clinical outcomes or mortality</cite>.

Bottom line: <cite id="5b4065d1-0">N-acetylcysteine is not effective as adjunctive treatment for severe falciparum malaria in this setting</cite>. While generally tolerated, <cite id="5b4065d1-0">possible interference with parasite clearance in artesunate-treated patients</cite> means it should not be considered a proven or routine oxidative-stress–targeted adjunct in severe malaria.

without_scope.text: What does clinical research indicate about the efficacy and safety of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as an adjunctive treatment targeting oxidative stress?
without_scope.answer:
Clinical research suggests that NAC has a <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">plausible role as a treatment or adjunct therapy for various medical conditions</cite> because it is being studied across disorders linked to redox imbalance, and <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">its safety, simplicity, and affordability</cite> make it attractive as an adjunct.

On efficacy, the clearest cross-condition clinical signal is that NAC can improve laboratory markers related to oxidative stress and inflammation. A systematic review/meta-analysis of controlled clinical trials found that <cite id="7d81a64b-4">NAC significantly decreased MDA, IL-8, and homocysteine levels</cite>, and that <cite id="7d81a64b-4">the effects of NAC on amending TNF-α and IL-6 levels were significant after subgroup analysis</cite>. That supports the idea that NAC can reduce oxidative-stress burden biologically, although biomarker improvement does not automatically mean large clinical benefit in every disease.

For clinical outcomes, the evidence is mixed and condition-specific rather than uniformly strong. A recent clinical review states that NAC’s efficacy is <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">well-established</cite> in some conventional indications such as <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">acetaminophen overdose, cystic fibrosis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease</cite>. Outside those uses, the same review says NAC <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">shows potential as an adjunctive treatment for a wide range of medical conditions</cite> and <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">may be beneficial</cite> in areas including reproductive, neurologic, gastrointestinal, and psychiatric disorders, but it also cautions that <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">evidence for some conditions is less robust</cite>. So the overall picture is “promising but not definitive” for many oxidative-stress-targeted adjunctive uses.

On safety, the evidence is generally favorable. NAC has <cite id="5f966d94-0">a well-established safety profile</cite>, and clinical data in respiratory disease indicate that <cite id="b4b297ab-0">studies with a dosage up to 3000 mg/day in respiratory diseases have shown that NAC is safe and well tolerated</cite>.

Bottom line: <cite id="7d81a64b-4">clinical trials/meta-analyses indicate NAC can improve oxidative-stress and inflammatory biomarkers</cite>, and <cite id="5f966d94-0">it is generally safe</cite>; however, <cite id="c3c83e5d-0">its clinical efficacy as an adjunctive treatment varies by condition, with stronger evidence in established indications and more preliminary or inconsistent evidence in many other diseases.</cite>

query.text: How does temperature quantitatively influence the development time and shedding patterns of Fasciola cercariae within their snail intermediate hosts?
query.answer: Temperature speeds up Fasciola development inside the snail in a strongly quantitative way: <cite id="5a3c720e-9">changes in temperature from 15–30°C reduced the sporocyst duration from 21 to 4 days</cite> and <cite id="5a3c720e-9">the redia duration from 37 to 11 days</cite>. Cercarial shedding also shows a clear thermal window: <cite id="f26f53ed-0">no cercariae shedding</cite> occurs <cite id="f26f53ed-0">at temperatures below 10°C or over 25°C</cite>, while <cite id="f26f53ed-1">the majority of cercariae shed at temperatures between 20–26°C</cite>; one review similarly identified <cite id="a883b7ad-0">10–26°C</cite> as the approximate critical minimum–maximum range for shedding. At the cold end, shedding is delayed and drawn out, because <cite id="5faec94d-0">cercariae shedding for Fasciola hepatica took longer at low temperatures (6–8°C)</cite>. When shedding does occur, it is not continuous but episodic: <cite id="5a3c720e-0">the snails shed their cercariae in one to 14 waves</cite>, with <cite id="5a3c720e-0">20.6%</cite> and <cite id="5a3c720e-0">15.7%</cite> of snails shedding in <cite id="5a3c720e-0">four and five periods respectively</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do the dosage and frequency of Dictyocaulus flagrans administration influence its effectiveness in reducing infective larvae in animals?

query.text: How do the dosage and frequency of Dictyocaulus flagrans administration influence its effectiveness in reducing infective larvae in animals?
query.answer: The evidence suggests that higher doses of Duddingtonia flagrans generally produce greater larval reduction, and administration does not always have to be daily to remain effective. - In horses, significant decreases in infective larvae from fecal cultures occurred only at doses of ≥3 × 104 spores/kg body weight, while survival through the digestive tract required doses of ≥6 × 105 chlamydospores/kg body weight. Also, daily administration of 3 × 105 spores/kg body weight reduced pasture infectivity by 57–100%. - In mouflon, daily dosing for 5 days at 5,000, 30,000, 150,000, and 750,000 spores/kg BW reduced infective larvae by 22.6% to 100%, and efficacy increased with dose rate, reaching ≥96% reduction at the three highest doses. - In calves, daily doses of 5 × 105, 10 × 105, and 20 × 105 spores/kg/day for 7 days led to increasing fecal spore recovery (11%, 29%, and 38%), and the fungus’s ability to trap and kill larvae increased significantly as dose level increased. - Longer-term daily or continuous administration is also effective: donkey foals given about 2.2 × 106 chlamydospores/kg BW/day throughout a transmission season showed 85–99% fewer infective larvae in feces and 70–100% fewer on herbage; calves continuously fed 3.5 × 105 to 1.4 × 106 chlamydospores/kg BW/day had significantly reduced pasture infectivity; and cattle treated daily for 6 months with pellets providing 3 × 104 chlamydospores/g had 57% fewer infective larvae in feces and 84% less on pasture. - Regarding frequency, cattle given 0.6 ×106, 3 ×106, or 15 ×106 chlamydospores/kg body weight at intervals of every 2 days, twice weekly, or every 4 days for 6 months all showed significant reductions in fecal L3. Importantly, no difference was found among treatment groups, and the interval between administrations can be extended while still significantly decreasing infective larvae and pasture contamination. Overall: effectiveness is dose-dependent up to a threshold, with higher doses usually giving stronger larval suppression, while frequency can often be reduced from daily to every few days without major loss of efficacy, at least in some cattle studies. So the best results typically come from adequate-to-high dosing delivered consistently over time, but strict daily administration is not always necessary.

without_term.answer:
In nematode-trapping fungi such as *Arthrobotrys* spp., temperature mainly changes <cite id="344b46b2-0">how many trapping nets are produced, what they look like, and how effective they are</cite> rather than being shown directly to control a well-defined “lifespan” of each individual net.

- <cite id="344b46b2-0">Trap formation is strongly temperature-dependent.</cite>
- In the 2024 study, <cite id="344b46b2-0">trap formation and nematocidal efficiency both “initially increased and then decreased with increasing temperature”</cite>, meaning there is an intermediate optimum rather than “hotter is always better.”
- The same study reports that <cite id="344b46b2-0">different temperatures produce different trap morphologies categorized as “NA,” “thin,” “dense,” and “sparse”</cite>; dense traps were associated with the best trapping performance.
- Another study on *A. oligospora* likewise found that <cite id="f858a81b-0">trap formation is highly temperature-dependent</cite> and that <cite id="f858a81b-0">the fungus cannot grow above 30°C</cite>, so excessively high temperatures would be expected to sharply reduce or eliminate trap production.

So, in plain terms: moderate temperatures tend to favor the formation of more robust, denser trapping nets, while temperatures that are too low or too high lead to fewer, thinner, sparser, or no nets at all. <cite id="344b46b2-0">The trend in net formation matches the trend in nematode-killing efficiency.</cite>

On longevity specifically: the sources retrieved here <cite id="344b46b2-0">describe changes in trap number, density, morphology, and efficiency with temperature</cite> but <cite id="f858a81b-0">do not provide a direct measurement of how long individual trapping nets persist before degrading.</cite> A cautious summary is that non-optimal temperatures likely shorten the functional persistence of traps indirectly by yielding sparse/poor traps or by impairing fungal growth, but the evidence above is stronger for formation than for net longevity.

questions.original_query: How are Hematodinium species classified taxonomically, and what morphological and genetic characteristics are used for their identification?

query.text: How are Hematodinium species classified taxonomically, and what morphological and genetic characteristics are used for their identification?
query.answer:
<cite id="b86f1f1e-0">Hematodinium perezi is classified as a dinoflagellate in the group Dinophyceae: Syndiniales.</cite> More broadly, <cite id="52544f27-0">Hematodinium spp. are dinoflagellate endoparasites of decapod crustaceans</cite>, and <cite id="af43c5f0-0">only two formally described species of Hematodinium were recognized in that review context</cite>, with additional lineages/genotypes often distinguished molecularly rather than solely by host.

For identification, the main morphological features are classic dinoflagellate traits. <cite id="37cce335-2">Hematodinium spp. can be identified as dinoflagellates on the basis of their typical dinokaryon (or mesokaryon) and alveolate pellicle</cite>. In ultrastructural studies, <cite id="b86f1f1e-0">H. perezi was confirmed by the presence of condensed chromatin profiles, trichocysts, an alveolar membrane, and micropores</cite>. The genus diagnosis also emphasizes <cite id="37cce335-4">the amphiesmal structure of the pellicle and condensed, beaded chromatin that forms V-shaped profiles</cite>. Early descriptions further noted <cite id="52544f27-0">multinucleate elongate plasmodia with characteristic dino-mitotic chromosomes</cite>.

Genetically, Hematodinium identification and discrimination rely mainly on ribosomal DNA markers. <cite id="af43c5f0-0">SSU rRNA, ITS, and LSU rRNA sequences</cite> are commonly used, and <cite id="90981ba6-0">Hematodinium sp. SSU rRNA, ITS, and LSU rRNA sequences</cite> have been used for comparative characterization. In practice, these markers help separate species or genotypes, because <cite id="b86f1f1e-0">molecular analysis of the ITS rRNA regions suggested different genotypes of H. perezi in crabs from different regions/hosts</cite>, and <cite id="37cce335-0">identification of Hematodinium species (and genotypes of H. perezi) is largely dependent upon geographical location rather than host species</cite>.

So, in short: Hematodinium species are treated as parasitic dinoflagellates within <cite id="b86f1f1e-0">Dinophyceae: Syndiniales</cite>, and they are identified using a combination of <cite id="37cce335-2,b86f1f1e-0,37cce335-4">morphological/ultrastructural characters such as the dinokaryon, alveolate pellicle, condensed chromatin, trichocysts, and micropores</cite> plus <cite id="af43c5f0-0,90981ba6-0">molecular markers from the ribosomal DNA region, especially SSU, ITS, and LSU sequences</cite>.

query.text: What do studies collectively indicate about the effect of acetazolamide co-administration on the timing of methotrexate clearance and its associated liver toxicity?
query.answer:
Collectively, the studies suggest that acetazolamide co-administration with high-dose methotrexate is associated with at least maintained, and possibly improved, methotrexate elimination rather than delayed clearance: supportive guidance states that <cite id="701634f0-0">adding acetazolamide when needed to keep urine pH > 7 “maximizes methotrexate elimination”</cite>, and a retrospective clearance study reported that <cite id="701634f0-2">utilizing acetazolamide may have reduced the average amount of sodium bicarbonate required for MTX clearance</cite>. 

On liver toxicity, the available evidence does not indicate a clear increase in methotrexate-associated hepatotoxicity from acetazolamide co-administration in these HDMTX studies; however, caution remains warranted because interaction references note that <cite id="c9cbd5bf-1">coadministration of methotrexate with other agents known to induce hepatotoxicity may potentiate the risk of liver injury</cite>, and acetazolamide itself has rare reports of liver injury <cite id="c9cbd5bf-3">including a case report of severe but asymptomatic DILI associated with acetazolamide use</cite>. 

So, in brief: <cite id="701634f0-0,701634f0-2">acetazolamide appears to support or at least not delay methotrexate clearance</cite>, while <cite id="c9cbd5bf-1,c9cbd5bf-3">evidence for added liver toxicity is limited and mostly precautionary rather than demonstrating a consistent clinical signal</cite>.

questions.original_query: What is the current evidence on the relationship between hypertension and serum Gd-IgA1 levels in patients?

query.text: What is the current evidence on the relationship between hypertension and serum Gd-IgA1 levels in patients?
query.answer: Current evidence suggests there is no clear, consistent relationship between hypertension and serum Gd-IgA1 levels in patients, mainly studied in IgA nephropathy (IgAN). The strongest summary comes from a 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 29 studies, which found that associations with hypertension, hematuria, and proteinuria were inconsistent and concluded that serum Gd-IgA1 levels were not associated with validated prognostic risk factors. A related search snippet from the same review reiterates that serum Gd-IgA1 levels were not associated with validated prognostic risk factors, but were negatively correlated with kidney function. So, the best current interpretation is: - Serum Gd-IgA1 is elevated in IgAN patients. - Its link to hypertension specifically is inconsistent and not established. - Evidence is stronger for an association with worse kidney function than with blood pressure/hypertension. In short: there is currently insufficient and inconsistent evidence that hypertensive patients have reliably higher serum Gd-IgA1 levels.

query.text: What do recent studies reveal about the impact of insulin resistance on myocardial reperfusion, plaque vulnerability, and mortality outcomes in patients undergoing PCI?
query.answer:
Recent studies suggest that insulin resistance in PCI patients is linked to worse outcomes across all three domains:

1. **Myocardial reperfusion after PCI**
   In non-diabetic STEMI patients treated with primary PCI, <cite id="157412146-0">acute insulin resistance (HOMA-IR >2.5 within 24 h) was present in 43% of patients</cite>, and <cite id="157412146-0">those with acute insulin resistance had lower rates of complete ST-segment resolution, lower myocardial blush grade, and lower left ventricular ejection fraction</cite>. Importantly, <cite id="157412146-0">HOMA-IR and glycemia were independent predictors of myocardial reperfusion as assessed by myocardial blush grade</cite>, and the study concluded that <cite id="157412146-0">acute insulin resistance after primary PCI is significantly associated with impaired myocardial reperfusion and larger infarct size</cite>.

2. **Plaque vulnerability**
   OCT-based evidence in CAD patients without diabetes shows that higher insulin resistance is associated with more unstable coronary plaque biology. Specifically, <cite id="809334464-0">patients with higher HOMA-IR had a higher prevalence of lipid-rich plaque, thin-cap fibroatheroma, and macrophage accumulation</cite>. The same study concluded that <cite id="809334464-0">high HOMA-IR values are associated with vulnerable plaque features and adverse clinical outcomes</cite>.

3. **Mortality and adverse outcomes after PCI**
   A recent systematic review/meta-analysis of post-PCI studies found that the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, a practical surrogate of insulin resistance, <cite id="32219298-0">potentially predicts adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI</cite>. Across <cite id="32219298-0">seven studies with 29,944 subjects</cite>, higher TyG was associated with <cite id="32219298-0">all-cause mortality (pooled adjusted RR 2.07, 95% CI 1.48–2.88)</cite>, as well as <cite id="32219298-0">major adverse cardiovascular events (RR 1.57), non-fatal MI (RR 1.27), and target vessel revascularization (RR 1.78)</cite>. The dose-response analysis further suggested that <cite id="32219298-0">each 1-unit increase in TyG was associated with an adjusted RR of 2.55 for all-cause mortality</cite>, although <cite id="32219298-0">the certainty of evidence was low or very low</cite>.

**Bottom line:** <cite id="157412146-0">Insulin resistance appears to impair microvascular/myocardial reperfusion after PCI</cite>, <cite id="809334464-0">is associated with more vulnerable coronary plaque morphology</cite>, and <cite id="32219298-0">is linked to higher mortality and recurrent ischemic events after PCI</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How have cohort studies assessed the risk of developing hypertension associated with anxiety disorders?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Cohort studies have generally assessed this question by <cite id="0ce8803f-0">following adults who were free of hypertension at baseline</cite> and comparing later hypertension incidence between those with and without anxiety, using <cite id="0ce8803f-0">adjusted odds ratios or hazard ratios</cite>.

Overall, the cohort evidence summarized in a 2015 systematic review/meta-analysis included <cite id="0ce8803f-0">eight prospective studies with a total sample size of 80,146 and 2,394 hypertension case subjects</cite>. Across these studies, the pooled estimate showed that <cite id="0ce8803f-0">anxiety was associated with higher risk of incident hypertension, with a pooled adjusted hazard ratio of 1.55 (95% CI 1.24–1.94)</cite>.

In terms of measurement, studies did not all define anxiety the same way. The review notes that prospective studies varied in their <cite id="0ce8803f-0">diagnostic criteria for anxiety</cite>, indicating that exposure was assessed using different anxiety definitions/instruments across cohorts. A concrete example is a 1-year prospective study in which anxiety exposure was measured using <cite id="d1e027d3-0">a structured psychiatric interview (PRIME-MD)</cite>. In that study, baseline hypertension exclusion relied on <cite id="d1e027d3-0">physician diagnosis of hypertension, and measured blood pressure</cite>, while incident hypertension at follow-up was determined by <cite id="d1e027d3-0">self-reported physician diagnosis</cite>.

That study found a relatively large short-term effect: <cite id="d1e027d3-0">having an anxiety disorder was associated with a 4-fold increase in the risk of developing hypertension (adjusted OR = 4.14, 95% CIs = 1.18–14.56)</cite>.

So, in summary: cohort studies have assessed the risk by prospectively tracking nonhypertensive participants, classifying baseline anxiety through clinical interviews or other diagnostic criteria, then estimating incident hypertension during follow-up with adjusted regression models; the pooled cohort evidence suggests <cite id="0ce8803f-0">an increased hypertension risk associated with anxiety</cite>, though <cite id="0ce8803f-0">heterogeneity was high (I² = 84.6%)</cite>.
